pool.q: What slit-lamp illumination technique is the most sensitive for detecting early guttae?
pool.rationale:
Endothelial imaging can be performed using various techniques. Specular reflection at the slit-lamp is the most sensitive slit-lamp technique for demonstrating early guttae. Other options include specular microscopy and confocal microscopy.
Direct illumination is useful for enhancing the visibility of raised lesions of the ocular surface and iris. Broad-beam illumination is optimal for visualizing eyelid lesions as well as the corneal opacities seen in dystrophies or scarring.
Sclerotic scatter is a form of indirect illumination and total internal reflection in the cornea; decentering the isocentric light beam so that an intense beam shines on the limbus and scatters off the sclera causes a very faint glow of the cornea. Reflective opacities stand out against the dark field, whereas areas of reduced light transmission in the cornea are seen as shades of gray. This technique is effective in demonstrating epithelial edema, mild stromal infiltration, nebulae, and cornea verticillata.
Retroillumination from the iris is performed by displacing the beam tangentially while examining the cornea. Through observing the zone between the light and dark backgrounds, the examiner can detect subtle corneal abnormalities. Retroillumination from the fundus is performed by aligning the light beam nearly parallel with the examiner’s visual axis and rotating the light so that it shines through the edge of the pupil. Opacities in the cornea, phakic or pseudophakic lens, or posterior capsule are highlighted against the red reflex, and iris defects can be transilluminated.

pool.q: A patient with keratoconus presents for evaluation of progressive visual loss. Glasses and contact lenses no longer fully correct his vision. He is interested in improving his vision but does not want to have a corneal transplant. What refractive procedure would be most appropriate for his condition?
pool.rationale: In corneal ectasias such as keratoconus, the cornea becomes thinner and weaker. PRK and LASIK are not preferred procedures by themselves, because the ablation of tissue increases the risk for ectasia progression and attendant poor refractive and structural outcomes. Corneal relaxing incisions also are not preferred to improve refractive demands, because they weaken the cornea, and the astigmatic error, which is often irregular in keratoconus, may not be amenable to correction with relaxing incisions. Intrastromal corneal ring segments such as Intacs can be implanted in the stroma to reduce refractive demands in patients with keratoconus, acting to flatten the cone and improve contact lens fitting.

pool.q: A 26-year-old man with a history of herpes simplex dendritic keratitis presents with ocular redness, photophobia, and blurred vision. Examination reveals corneal stromal edema, keratic precipitates, and an anterior chamber reaction. The corneal epithelium is intact. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.b: Administer trifluridine drops and oral acyclovir.
options.c: Administer prednisolone acetate drops and oral acyclovir.
options.d: Perform corneal cultures for herpes simplex and bacteria; treat with trifluridine drops and fluoroquinolone drops.

pool.rationale: Recommendations of the Herpetic Eye Disease Study (HEDS) included treating stromal herpetic disease with topical corticosteroids together with a prophylactic antiviral medication to reduce persistence or progression of stromal inflammation and shorten the duration of herpes simplex virus (HSV) stromal disease. Because of the absence of ocular side effects, prophylactic oral acyclovir is preferred by many to trifluridine drops. Topically applied antivirals are not absorbed by the cornea through intact corneal epithelium. HEDS showed no additional benefit when oral acyclovir was added to trifluridine and prednisolone in the treatment for herpetic stromal keratitis. Although bacterial superinfections are rare, in nonresponsive cases subsequent stromal cultures for Acanthamoeba may be warranted.

pool.q: A 41-year-old patient with no significant ocular history presents with unilateral photophobia and blurred vision for 1 week. Examination reveals intact epithelium with a focal area of corneal edema with large underlying keratic precipitates. A 2+ cellular anterior chamber reaction is present. What is the most likely etiology?
pool.rationale:
The presentation described is consistent with disciform keratitis, the most common cause of which is herpes simplex virus.
Adenovirus can present as severe unilateral or bilateral conjunctivitis, typically with conjunctival membranes. Subepithelial infiltrates develop after the acute phase resolves.
EBV presents with multifocal subepithelial or deep infiltrates, similar to post epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC). Diagnosis is based on recent history of EBV or high titers.
CMV typically causes retinitis; however, some anterior findings, such as anterior uveitis and endotheliitis, can be found.

pool.q: A patient has peripheral ulcerative keratitis (PUK) with threatened perforation due to rheumatoid arthritis. What is the next step?

options.a: cyanoacrylate glue and bandage contact lens
options.d: scraping of thinned area to remove inflammatory factors

pool.rationale:
Definitive management of PUK often cannot be achieved by local measures alone. It may require institution or escalation of systemic treatment, including immunosuppression with oral prednisone, cytotoxic agents such as cyclophosphamide, or immunomodulatory agents such as methotrexate or cyclosporine. Biologic agents such as infliximab have reportedly been used with some success. Threatened perforation should be treated with temporizing measures such as cyanoacrylate glue and bandage contact lens placement until systemic therapy has been initiated.
Conjunctival flaps are best avoided in immune-mediated disease, because bringing the conjunctival vasculature closer to the area of corneal disease could accelerate melting. Interferon therapy is sometimes helpful in hepatitis C-associated cases of Mooren ulcer-type PUK. Scraping of the cornea is not indicated in this case of threatened perforation, because it may turn into a full perforation.

pool.q: Two days ago, a 27-year-old man's left eye was struck by an opponent's thumb during a basketball game. Now, he has light sensitivity, blurred vision, and conjunctival injection. His slit-lamp examination reveals 1+ cells in the anterior chamber. What treatment is recommended?
pool.rationale:
This man has a traumatic iritis from his athletic efforts. Photophobia, tearing, and ocular pain may occur within 24 hours after injury. The inflammation of traumatic iritis is often associated with diminished vision and perilimbal conjunctival injection. The anterior chamber reaction can be surprisingly minimal but is usually present if carefully sought. Treatment should consist of, at the very least, a topical cycloplegic agent to relieve patient discomfort. Topical corticosteroids can be used if significant inflammation is present. Once the iritis has diminished, cycloplegia can be discontinued, and topical corticosteroids should be tapered slowly to prevent rebound iritis.
Treatment with oral steroids is not usually necessary for mild traumatic uveitis. Hypertonic saline may be indicated for patients with recurrent corneal erosion, but it is not likely to be helpful or comforting for patients with traumatic iritis. Antibiotic drops are not therapeutic for iritis.

pool.q: What range of myopia can intracorneal ring segments (ICRSs) treat?
pool.rationale:
The correct answer is mild levels of myopia. Corneal ring segments are approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to treat mild levels of myopia (-1.00 to -3.00 D). They are not indicated for the treatment of astigmatism. While not commonly used for the treatment of myopia anymore, they are most commonly used for patients with keratoconus (KCN). They are contraindicated in patients with autoimmune disease, immunodeficiency, or collagen vascular disease; in pregnant or nursing women; or in the presence of significant corneal pathology. The rings are inserted after the creation of an intrastromal channel by either mechanical means or femtosecond laser ablation.
Patients must be older than 21 years of age, experience a decline in visual acuity that limits functional abilities, have clear central corneas, and have a corneal thickness greater than 450 microns at the channel site. Complications can include bothersome white deposits around the ring segments, sterile or microbial keratitis, implant extrusion or penetration into the eye, corneal thinning, induced astigmatism, iritis, monocular diplopia, and poor night vision.

pool.q: What is the most common presentation for herpes simplex conjunctivitis in an immunocompetent patient?
pool.rationale:
Herpes simplex conjunctivitis causes a follicular conjunctivitis that is almost always unilateral (except in immunocompromised hosts or patients with atopic disease). Also of note, when it is the first event of ocular infection, ocular herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection typically manifests as blepharoconjunctivitis. Epithelial keratitis may also occur during a primary ocular HSV infection; however, stromal keratitis or uveitis would be atypical.
Bilateral follicular conjunctivitis is more typically seen in adenoviral conjunctivitis. Papillary conjunctivitis is typically caused by allergic, bacterial, or mechanical factors.

pool.q: A 57-year-old woman has confluent guttae in both eyes. She complains of intermittent, transient blurred vision in the OS on waking. Her best-corrected acuity is 20/25 OD and 20/30 OS at 8 AM. What would an appropriate course of management be?

options.c: hypertonic sodium chloride ointment OS at night

pool.rationale:
The description is typical of early Fuchs endothelial dystrophy. The most commonly used treatments for early Fuchs are hyperosmotic agents (5% sodium chloride); drops during the day and ointment at night may reduce edema upon awakening. Another option is a hair dryer set on cool.
Bandage soft contact lenses can be used to treat painful erosions and ruptured bullae, but they are not routinely used to treat early morning edema. Surgical options are considered in more advanced disease, with the first-line therapy being endothelial replacement surgery in those without significant stromal scarring.

pool.q: A patient is diagnosed with acute viral follicular conjunctivitis. The patient starts using preservative-free tears and returns in 1 week with bilateral loss of vision, worse in the right than the left eye. His best-corrected visual acuity is 20/40 OD and 20/30 OS. What is the most likely finding on his slit-lamp examination?
pool.rationale:
Although most cases of adenoviral conjunctivitis are self-limited, epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC) is distinguished by significant corneal involvement. Within 7 to 14 days after onset of symptoms, multifocal subepithelial corneal infiltrates can appear, associated with decreased vision and photophobia. Other complications of EKC include geographic corneal erosions, pseudomembranes and membranes with eventual conjunctival scarring, symblepharon, and chronic dry eye. Anterior chamber cell would be more common in other conditions, including HSV keratoconjunctivitis. Geographic ulceration is also more characteristic of HSV keratitis. Corneal stromal melts can be associated with numerous conditions (neurotrophic cornea, collagen vascular disease, infectious keratopathy) but is not characteristic of EKC.

pool.q: A 56-year-old patient with herpes simplex dendritic keratitis was treated with topical trifluridine, 9 times per day for 3 weeks. The dendrite resolved, but the patient developed marked punctate epithelial keratopathy and epithelial irregularity. The corneal stroma is clear. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.a: Discontinue topical trifluridine and add lubricants.
options.b: Discontinue topical trifluridine and add vidarabine ointment.
options.c: Continue topical trifluridine and add oral prednisone.
options.d: Culture the cornea for herpes simplex virus and add topical tobramycin.

pool.rationale: Topical trifluridine is toxic to the corneal epithelium and discontinuation after 10 to 14 days is generally recommended. If epithelial irregularities persist due to prolonged exposure, the treatment is to discontinue trifluridine and begin using topical lubricants. Adding oral prednisone will have no effect on epithelial integrity. Similarly, vidarabine and tobramycin are not useful in the scenario presented.

pool.q: Primary Sjögren syndrome can be differentiated from secondary Sjögren syndrome using what method?
pool.rationale: Primary Sjögren syndrome is defined by the absence of a predisposing autoimmune condition (eg, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus). Secondary Sjögren syndrome occurs in patients with a well-defined, generalized, connective tissue disease. Both primary and secondary subsets of patients can present with abnormal (decreased) Schirmer tear testing, dry mouth, and positive lip biopsy results. For this reason, a systemic rheumatologic evaluation is necessary to differentiate primary from secondary Sjögren syndrome.

pool.q: What is an appropriate therapy for gonococcal conjunctivitis without corneal ulceration in an adult?

options.b: intramuscular ceftriaxone or oral ciprofloxacin on an outpatient basis with close follow-up

pool.rationale: Hyperacute conjunctivitis is usually due to Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Management of gonococcal conjunctivitis requires systemic treatment, with topical antibiotics used as adjunctive therapy only. Options for adjunctive topical treatment include erythromycin ointment, bacitracin ointment, gentamicin ointment, and ciprofloxacin solution. Aggressive cases required copious irrigation of the conjunctival sac every 30 to 60 minutes. Current treatment recommendations incorporate concern for the increasing prevalence of penicillin-resistant N gonorrhoeae (PRNG). Adults can be managed on an outpatient regimen of intramuscular ceftriaxone or oral ciprofloxacin. Up to one-third of patients with gonococcal conjunctivitis are reported to also have Chlamydia trachomatis and can require additional antibiotic coverage. Corneal ulceration and perforation can occur quickly, so very close follow-up is required.

pool.q: What technique should be avoided in pterygium excision surgery?
pool.rationale: Several options are available to repair the defect left in the conjunctiva after pterygium removal. These include free conjunctival autograft, sliding conjunctival pedicle flap, and/or amniotic membrane graft. Leaving the area bare is not advised, as this increases the risk of pterygium recurrence. The rate of recurrence with bare sclera is 32% to 88%.

pool.q: What condition is typified by stromal opacification with corneal thinning but with an intact corneal epithelium?
pool.rationale:
Terrien marginal corneal degeneration and senile furrow degeneration present as nonulcerative opacities (eg, stromal opacification with corneal thinning but intact corneal epithelium).
Phlyctenulosis, rosacea keratitis, and vernal and atopic keratoconjunctivitis present as nonulcerative keratitis (eg, stromal inflammation without an epithelial defect). Traumatic corneal abrasion, toxic keratopathy, and neurotrophic keratopathy are all examples of conditions where there is a corneal epithelial defect without stromal inflammation. Mooren ulcer is an example of a nonsuppurative ulcerative keratitis and, when active, presents with an epithelial defect.

pool.q: A patient presents with a pigmented conjunctival lesion, which he notes has enlarged over the past 3 months. What is the most appropriate management option?
pool.rationale: Periodic observation with sequential photographs is a reasonable option for stable melanocytic lesions. For pigmented lesions with documented growth, however, excisional biopsy (and not incisional biopsy) is the preferred approach. Diagnostic results can determine the need for further treatment, including surgery, cryotherapy, radiotherapy, or chemotherapy.

pool.q: Sectoral iris atrophy frequently accompanies what inflammatory condition?
pool.rationale:
Sectoral atrophy of the iris is commonly seen during varicella-zoster infection.
Although herpes simplex infections may also be accompanied by iris atrophy, the pattern of atrophy is patchy.
Iris atrophy may be seen following chronic treatment of Acanthamoeba keratitis, but the condition is secondary to the toxicity of the therapies and is not a primary effect of the infection. Iris atrophy is not seen in rosacea keratitis.

pool.q: What is the current recommendation with regard to using corneal tissue from a donor with suspected Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease?

options.a: There is no restriction on using donor tissue from patients with Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.
options.b: The tissue is disqualified only if the donor has biopsy-proven Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.
options.c: The tissue is disqualified from all transplantation uses.
options.d: The tissue can be used for endothelial keratoplasty, but it is disqualified from full-thickness corneal transplantation.

pool.rationale:
Prion diseases can be transmitted through any type of transplanted human tissue, so patients in whom prion diseases are suspected (even without biopsy confirmation) are automatically disqualified from organ transplantation status. At least 1 confirmed case of Creutzfeldt-Jakob case transmitted by corneal tissue has been reported.

pool.q: What portion of the average cornea is the steepest?

options.a: The central cornea is steeper than the peripheral cornea.
options.b: There is variable surface curvature throughout the cornea.
options.c: The corneal surface curvature does not change significantly from the center to the periphery.
options.d: The peripheral cornea is steeper than the central cornea.

pool.rationale: The central corneal thickness is approximately 540-550 microns, which is significantly thinner than the peripheral corneal thickness of approximately 650-1000 microns. This is mostly due to the fact that the posterior surface of the cornea has a smaller radius of curvature than the anterior surface. The central cornea is steeper than the peripheral cornea. It is worth noting that there is a lot of variability in the literature regarding the thickness of the peripheral cornea, and the Basic and Clinical Science Course (BCSC) notes a peripheral thickness of 650-1000 microns.

pool.q: Why is tissue from donors younger than 2 years generally not used in corneal transplantation?

options.a: There are ethical concerns about using tissue from infants and very young children.
options.b: The corneal endothelial cells are not sufficiently developed.
options.c: The tissue is steeply curved and flaccid.
options.d: The corneal stroma is too thin.

pool.rationale: Most eye banks accept corneal tissue from donors 2 to 75 years of age. Tissue from donors younger than 2 years is typically not used because it is extremely steeply curved and flaccid. This makes the tissue difficult to handle and poses challenges for the surgeon in creating a watertight closure and achieving a predictable outcome.

pool.q: What is the pathology of Meesmann corneal dystrophy?

options.b: intraepithelial cysts consisting of degenerated epithelial products
options.c: disruption of the Bowman layer and replacement by a sheetlike connective tissue layer
options.d: diffuse cytoplasmic vacuolization of affected cells

pool.rationale: Intraepithelial cysts consisting of degenerated epithelial products occur in Meesmann corneal dystrophy. Diffuse cytoplasmic vacuolization of affected cells occurs in Lisch epithelial corneal dystrophy. Subepithelial and stromal amyloid deposits occur in gelatinous droplike corneal dystrophy. Disruption of the Bowman layer and replacement by a sheetlike connective tissue layer occurs in Reis-Bücklers corneal dystrophy.

pool.q: What feature characterizes pellucid marginal degeneration?

options.d: corneal protrusion at area of maximal thinning

pool.rationale: Pellucid marginal degeneration is characterized by protrusion above a band of inferior peripheral thinning in the absence of inflammation. In keratoconus, corneal protrusion occurs at the area of maximal thinning. Peripheral neovascularization and corneal lipid deposition are not characteristic of pellucid marginal degeneration.

pool.q: What material are intrastromal corneal ring segments made from?
pool.rationale: Intrastromal corneal ring segments are made of polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA).

pool.q: In a patient with a worsening posttraumatic corneal ulcer and negative scrapings, what is the best next step in managing the condition?

options.a: Start the patient on a program of empiric topical steroids.
options.c: Start the patient on a program of empiric systemic steroids.

pool.rationale: Posttraumatic corneal ulcers can be polymicrobial and/or be associated with inoculation by unusual bacteria, fungi, or other microorganisms. When faced with a worsening clinical picture, corneal biopsy is indicated. The use of empiric steroids when the organism(s) may not be known is generally not advised. The likelihood of a viral superinfection in a post-traumatic setting is low and would miss more immediate infectious dangers.

pool.q: What risk is lower in deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty (DALK) than in penetrating keratoplasty (PK)?
pool.rationale:
The primary advantage of deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty (DALK) over penetrating keratoplasty (PK) is the preservation of the host endothelium and avoidance of the "open sky" condition during surgery. The "big-bubble" technique relies on pneumatic dissection of the host Descemet membrane.
As there is no penetration into the anterior chamber, lamellar keratoplasty has lower risks of cystoid macular edema (CME), glaucoma, cataract, expulsive hemorrhage, retinal detachment (RD), and endophthalmitis.
Lamellar keratoplasty can be associated with irregular astigmatism, stromal rejection (but not endothelial rejection), and interface opacification and vascularization (which is not a risk in PK as there is no interface).

pool.q: What is the most common ocular neoplasm in patients affected by xeroderma pigmentosum?
pool.rationale:
Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common ocular neoplasm in patients with xeroderma pigmentosum.
Xeroderma pigmentosum is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by the inability to repair ultraviolet (UV) light-damaged DNA. It has skin manifestations of hyperpigmentation, actinic keratosis, and telangiectasias, which can appear prior to skin neoplasms. Similarly, ocular manifestations in addition to dry eyes can include pingueculae and pterygia. Also, 11% of xeroderma patients are affected by ocular neoplasms, with squamous cell carcinoma being the most common. These patients need UV protection and careful monitoring for skin and ocular neoplasms.

pool.q: A patient with a history of penetrating keratoplasty 3 years prior presents with decreased vision and increased photophobia. Slit-lamp examination reveals an area of corneal edema on the graft with an underlying, linear collection of inflammatory precipitates. The graft epithelium is intact. What is the most appropriate treatment?
pool.rationale: The slit-lamp finding of graft edema with an underlying, linear collection of inflammatory precipitates is classic for a Khodadoust line. The most likely diagnosis in this case is graft rejection and should be treated promptly with frequent topical steroids. Graft edema with intact epithelium is less likely to be due to active keratitis and treatment with acyclovir (herpes simplex virus [HSV]), chlorhexidine (acanthamoeba), or moxifloxacin (bacteria) will not be effective.

pool.q: What is the best culture media for Acanthamoeba?
pool.rationale: Acanthamoeba is best cultured on nonnutrient agar with an overlay of killed Enterobacter aerogenes or Escherichia coli. Alternatively, Acanthamoeba can sometimes be recognized by trails left by trophozoites on blood agar. Löwenstein-Jensen agar is best used for isolating mycobacteria. Sabouraud agar is best used for isolating fungi. Thioglycollate broth is best used to isolating aerobic and anaerobic bacteria.

pool.q: If Acanthamoeba keratitis is suspected, but cultures have not been positive, what is another diagnostic step that can help visualize the organism, especially the cyst forms?

options.a: high-resolution anterior segment optical coherence tomography (OCT)
options.b: corneal biopsy followed by examination with acid fast technique

pool.rationale:
Diagnosis of Acanthamoeba can be made with positive cultures from corneal scrapings grown on nonnutrient agar with E coli or Enterobacter aerogenes overlay, or buffered charcoal-yeast extract agar. Characteristic trails form since the trophozoites are motile and travel across the surface of the culture plate. However, culture yield only ranges from 35% to 50% in larger studies. Thus, many cases are treated based on clinical suspicion (see below for review of clinical features). If available, another option for diagnosis is the use of in vivo confocal microscopy, which is a noninvasive imaging tool to visualize the organism in the cornea, in particular the cyst forms (see figure), though trophozoites can also be seen. In vivo means no corneal sample needs to be taken; the imaging is completed on the patient through his or her cornea.
When scrapings are done, smears are also made with stains to visualize the amebae. If diagnosis is still not definitive with all the above, a lamellar corneal biopsy may be required to obtain more tissue. Acid-fast stain is not used for Acanthamoeba. The amebae are visualized with Giemsa or with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS), calcofluor white, or acridine orange stain. Acid-fast stains should be used in suspected mycobacteria and/or Nocardia cases.
Anterior segment OCT does not yet have sufficient resolution to demonstrate acanthamoeba cysts. An anterior chamber tap is not warranted, and in fact should be avoided, because it may inadvertently seed organisms into the eye.
CLINICAL FEATURES
  • history of contact lens use, exposure to possibly contaminated freshwater or soil
  • severe eye pain (disproportional to signs)
  • photophobia
  • protracted, progressive course
  • bilateral in 7-11%
  • no response to many topical antimicrobial agents
  • Early signs:
    1. If localized to corneal epithelium, diffuse punctate epitheliopathy or dendritic epithelial lesion (misdiagnosed as herpetic keratitis*)
    2. If stromal infection: usually central cornea, gray-white superficial, nonsuppurative infiltrate
  • Later sign:
    1. central, partial or complete, ring infiltrate
  • Inflamed corneal nerves (called radial perineuritis or radial keratoneuritis): nearly pathognomonic
  • Limbitis
  • Scleritis (focal, nodular or diffuse)
  • Dacryoadenitis
  • Intraocular extension may occur
*More likely Acanthamoeba if noncontiguous or multifocal pattern of granular epitheliopathy and subepithelial opacities (HSV contiguous, dendritic pattern), disproportionately severe ocular pain (HSV disproportionately mild pain secondary to trigeminal nerve involvement), risk factors present including contact lens or possible contaminated freshwater, and failure to respond to initial antiviral therapy.

pool.q: A 25-year-old woman with a recent history of the flu was treated by her primary care physician for "pink eye" with gentamicin eye drops 4 times a day. Five days later the patient presents with increased eye redness, eyelid itching, and epiphora. Slit-lamp examination reveals peripheral infiltrates in the epithelium and anterior stroma with a clear zone between the lesions and the limbus. What is the appropriate management?

options.a: start trifluridine drops every 2 hours while the patient is awake
options.b: start moxifloxacin drops 4 times per day and stop gentamicin
options.c: increase the frequency of the gentamicin to every hour

pool.rationale:
This presentation is highly suggestive of a toxic reaction to topical gentamicin. The initial symptoms (conjunctivitis following a flu-like illness) were likely viral and the worsening symptoms (particularly eyelid irritation or eczema) after starting topical gentamicin favor an allergic etiology for the clinical deterioration. Toxic reaction to aminoglycosides can even present as peripheral infiltrates in the epithelium and anterior stroma, with a clear zone between the lesions and the limbus. The most appropriate response is to discontinue the offending agent and prescribe preservative-free artificial tears. Increasing the gentamicin would be counterproductive. Topical trifluridine would only be indicated for herpetic corneal disease. Moxifloxacin is a typical antibiotic used for bacterial infections.

pool.q: A patient reports a foreign body sensation after hammering sheet metal. No foreign body is identified. What should be the next step of the examination?

options.d: Perform anterior segment optical coherence tomography (OCT).

When assessing a patient with a potential foreign body, it is important to always evert the upper lids. Gonioscopy and anterior segment OCT may be indicated for other reasons, but not in visualizing a foreign body on the ocular surface. MRI is contraindicated if a metallic foreign body is suspected. Evaluation of a patient with traumatic ocular injury should include a complete general and ophthalmic examination.

pool.q: For primary pterygium excision, what surgical technique has been shown to provide the lowest recurrence rate?
pool.rationale: Pterygium excision with a free conjunctival autograft is associated with the lowest recurrence rate following pterygium surgery (0%-4%). Both rotational and primary conjunctival closure methods have performed less favorably, with recurrence rates as high as 39%. Excision with bare sclera is associated with the highest risk of recurrence (up to 88%) and is not a preferred method of treatment. Alternative methods that have been used include amniotic membrane grafting (which may be comparable to conjunctival autografting, although the current literature still tends to favor free conjunctival autografting), or excision with bare sclera and application of mitomycin C (which may increase the odds of other postoperative complications, including delayed wound healing and scleral melting or infectious scleritis).

pool.q: A 25-year-old diabetic patient presents with a 1-week history of eye pain, redness, and decreased vision. She states that she scratched her eye with her fingernail 1 week ago. Examination reveals a purulent discharge, with a bulbar conjunctival epithelial defect and underlying scleral necrosis. The cornea is clear. What is the most appropriate therapy?
pool.rationale: The description is consistent with a microbial scleritis, likely arising from the previous fingernail injury. The patient's history of diabetes raises the concern for immunocompromise. Therapy should consist of topical broad-spectrum antibiotics, ideally after obtaining cultures for bacterial and fungal pathogens. Cyclophosphamide and corticosteroids are appropriate therapies for immunologically driven forms of scleritis, but in this case a bacterial etiology should be suspected prior to initiating immunosuppressive therapy. Oral NSAIDs can be beneficial for episcleritis or mild anterior scleritis.

pool.q: What fungus is most likely to cause fungal keratitis in immunosuppressed patients?
pool.rationale:
Candida

Fungal keratitis in patients with a compromised immune status (eg, diabetes mellitus, chronic illness) is typically caused by a yeast such as Candida. Candida albicans is the most common yeast at these sites. Tissue penetration of the cornea is facilitated by pseudohyphae, which express proteases and phospholipases. Aspergillus and Fusarium are septate filamentous fungi that most commonly infect the eye as a result of trauma with soil or vegetable matter, or with contact lens usage. Streptomyces is a genus of gram-positive bacteria that resembles filamentous fungi, and may produce an indolent keratitis that resembles mycotic keratitis.

pool.q: A patient has watery discharge and itching preceding development of conjunctival papillae. What kind of conjunctivitis is she most likely to have?
pool.rationale:
Intense itching is a hallmark symptom and a classic complaint most commonly associated with allergic conjunctivitis. Symptoms develop rapidly after allergen exposure and consist of itching, eyelid swelling, conjunctival hyperemia, chemosis, and mucoid discharge. Attacks are usually short lived and episodic.
Viral, bacterial, and toxic conjunctivitis are typically associated with burning or irritating sensations.

pool.q: After surgical removal of a pterygium, what is the best approach to minimize the risk of recurrence and avoid any late-term complications?
pool.rationale:
Several studies have demonstrated that the risk of recurrence after pterygium excision is lower if a conjunctival autograft, rather than an amniotic membrane transplant, is used. However, if the defect created following dissection of the pterygium is considerably larger than what can be covered with an autologous conjunctival graft, an amniotic membrane graft or simple limbal epithelial transplantation (SLET) are viable options to cover the entire area of resection. Covering the entire defect decreases postoperative inflammation and speeds re-epithelialization of the ocular surface.
Although there is evidence that the use of MMC with conjunctival autografting reduces the pterygium recurrence rate after surgical excision, further studies are necessary to determine the optimal route of administration and dose for MMC as well as the duration of treatment with MMC and its long-term effects. Any use of topical MMC can be toxic and might cause visually significant complications, such as aseptic scleral necrosis and infectious sclerokeratitis. These complications might occur months, or even years, after use of the drug. The use of bevacizumab in primary pterygium excision apparently has no effect on the recurrence rate of this condition.

pool.q: What suture is recommended for surgical repair of the limbus portion of a corneoscleral laceration?
pool.rationale:
The preferred type of suture for repair of the limbal portion of corneoscleral lacerations is 9-0 or 10-0 nylon. Nylon suture is monofilament and nonabsorbable, which provides prolonged wound support with minimal induction of inflammation.
Polyglactin (commonly referred to by the brand name Vicryl) suture is absorbable and braided, which can lead to premature loss of wound support and increased inflammation. For scleral wound closure, 8-0 silk or 9-0 nylon suture can be used.

pool.q: A 61-year-old woman, referred with dry eyes, has 20/60 visual acuity in both eyes with diffuse punctate staining and whorled epithelium. The Schirmer test is normal and tear breakup time is greater than 10 seconds. She has been using generic artificial tears 4 times daily in addition to latanoprost and timolol in both eyes. What would be appropriate initial management?

options.a: bilateral occlusion of the lower puncta
options.b: increasing the frequency of artificial tear use
options.c: providing preservative-free alternatives for all drops

pool.rationale: This patient has bilateral punctate staining with whorled epithelium in the absence of aqueous tear deficiency and evaporative dry eye. These clinical findings, along with her use of multiple eyedrops, are suggestive of toxic keratitis; benzalkonium chloride, the preservative found in most eyedrops, is a common offender. Switching to preservative-free alternatives is likely to improve the ocular surface. Adding topical steroids, increasing the frequency of generic artificial tears (which generally contain preservatives), or performing punctal occlusion would all increase exposure to preservatives and could worsen the condition.

pool.q: What is the preferred medium for culturing mycobacteria?
pool.rationale:
Aerobic bacteria grow best on blood agar, chocolate agar, and in thioglycollate broth. Anaerobic bacteria grow best on anaerobic blood agar, phenylethyl alcohol agar in an anaerobic chamber, and thioglycollate or chopped meat broth. Mycobacteria grow on blood agar and Löwenstein-Jensen agar. (Middlebrook agar is also used, however this is not listed in the BCSC). Fungi grow on blood agar (25ºC), Sabouraud dextrose agar with antibacterial agent (25ºC), and brain-heart infusion agar (25ºC). Acanthamoeba organisms grow on nonnutrient agar with bacterial overlay, blood agar, and buffered charcoal-yeast extract agar.
When it is necessary to send cultures for mycobacteria (species divided into 2 groups by growth rate, both grow on Löwenstein-Jensen medium and blood agar):
Scleritis (microbial scleritis is very rare)
  • mycobacterium tuberculosis (slow growers) and atypical mycobacteria (fast growers)
  • tuberculous scleritis - consider in chronic, steroid-dependent scleritis or in surgically induced necrotizing scleritis (SINS)
Keratitis
  • atypical mycobacteria (fast growers): M fortuitum and M cheloneae (found in soil and water)
  • immunocompromised ocular surface
  • infections following laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) - delayed onset of ulcerative keratitis after refractive surgery, refractory to treatment, nonsuppurative infiltrates, treat with oral and topical clarithromycin, amikacin, linezolid, and fluoroquinolones with antimycobacterial activity (moxifloxacin, besifloxacin, and gatifloxacin).
*Of note, atypical mycobacteria have been supplanted by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) as the most common cause of keratitis after refractive surgery, however they are still an important cause of post-refractive surgery keratitis.
Uveitis
  • M tuberculosis
  • isolated granulomatous anterior uveitis (exceedingly uncommon if no posterior segment disease)
  • usually granulomatous with mutton-fat keratic precipitates, iris nodules, posterior synechiae, secondary glaucoma, nongranulomatous can happen, too
  • vitreous opacities and cystoid macular edema
  • disseminated choroiditis is the most common presentation
  • retina involved usually as extension of choroidal disease, can have a retinal vasculitis/Eales disease (peripheral retinal perivasculitis)
  • histologically proven intraocular TB found in pulmonary and extrapulmonary infections, and in symptomatic and asymptomatic patients (the clinician must ask the patient in the review of systems for fever, night sweats, weight loss)
  • high-risk groups: health care professionals, recent immigrants from endemic areas, the indigent, immunocompromised patients (chronic disease, HIV/AIDS, or on immunomodulatory therapy), and older adults

(A figure accompanies this rationale on the section page.)

pool.q: What is the most effective topical therapy for keratitis caused by Acanthamoeba species?
pool.rationale:
Acanthamoeba is a protozoal infection that can present in many ways. However, severe ocular pain, a ring infiltrate, and radial perineuritis are some of the more distinct features.
Topical biguanides (polyhexamethylene biguanide [polyhexanide] or chlorhexidine) are the most effective treatment against Acanthamoeba keratitis.
Aminoglycosides (including amikacin) and triazoles may have some limited efficacy as adjunctive therapy but are less effective than biguanides. Fluoroquinolones have no role in the treatment of Acanthamoeba.

pool.q: For the past week, a 69-year-old woman has had tingling over her right eyelid and forehead, followed by lid edema and a vesicular rash, which respects the vertical midline and involves the tip of her nose. What is her most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale: The symptoms of paresthesias and a vesicular rash in the first division of the trigeminal nerve, respecting the midline in an elderly patient, likely represents herpes zoster dermatitis, with a previous history of childhood varicella zoster. Herpes simplex does not present with dermatomal distribution. Mycosis fungoides, a cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, presents with a diffuse rash that is not vesicular or acute. Basal cell carcinoma also presents in an indolent fashion and in a discrete way.

pool.q: What is the purpose of rose bengal staining?
pool.rationale: Rose bengal is a vital dye that stains damaged or devitalized epithelial cells. The technique is the same as for fluorescein, but it is important to caution the patient that rose bengal dye may burn. Rose bengal is particularly useful for assessing damage and wound healing in dry eye, exposure, medication toxicity, superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis, herpes simplex virus, and varicella zoster virus. Fluorescein is preferred for detecting wound leaks, measuring tear breakup times, and evaluating for corneal epithelial defects.

pool.q: On slit-lamp examination, a patient is found to have easy upper eyelid eversion. In addition to evaluating the patient for keratoconus, what study should be ordered?

options.c: computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)

pool.rationale:
Floppy eyelid syndrome consists of easily everted upper eyelids with chronic papillary conjunctivitis. It has been associated with keratoconus, eyelid rubbing, obesity, and sleep apnea. Because of the association with sleep apnea and the health risk with apneic episodes, it is important to refer these patients for a sleep study so they can be treated, as needed (eg, with continuous positive airway pressure [CPAP] therapy). Ocular treatment options include aggressive lubrication, taping or shielding eyelids during sleep, and horizontal eyelid tightening. Patients should be encouraged to lose weight.
Carotid Doppler studies are helpful for patients who develop ocular ischemic syndrome. Patients with this syndrome will present with gradual or sudden visual loss or amaurosis fugax. The ocular findings may include rubeosis, corneal edema, anterior chamber cell and flare, vitreous cells, neovascularization, optic disc pallor, optic nerve swelling, cherry red spot, and retinal hemorrhages in the midperiphery. If a patient is found to have ocular ischemic syndrome, treatment options include lowering intraocular pressure, carotid endarterectomy (if patient has severe stenosis), or panretinal photocoagulation (PRP).
Patients with floppy eyelid syndrome may have a higher rate of atherosclerosis secondary to their obesity, but a carotid Doppler test would not be indicated unless the patient had other symptoms. A single-fiber EMG is a useful diagnostic tool for neuromuscular disorders, especially myasthenia gravis (MG). MG is a weakness of voluntary muscles due to antibodies blocking Ach receptors. MG patients will have intermittent, asymmetric ptosis but is not associated with easy upper eyelid eversion. Other diagnostic tests for MG include the tensilon test, Ach receptor antibody test, ice test, or rest test. MG is treated with mestinon (AChE inhibitor), steroids, plasmapheresis, intravenous gamma globulin, or thymectomy.
A single-fiber EMG test result in a floppy eyelid syndrome patient would be normal. A CT or MRI of the orbits would not help diagnose floppy eyelid syndrome.

pool.q: What immunoglobulin class predominantly mediates the pathophysiology of seasonal allergic conjunctivitis?
pool.rationale: Seasonal allergic conjunctivitis is predominantly driven by an IgE-mediated hypersensitivity response. Allergens activate mast cells via IgE antibodies. Activation of these antibodies triggers the release of histamine and other inflammatory mediators, producing the characteristic response of edema, vasodilation, and itching.

pool.q: What is the predominant mechanism of injury following an alkali chemical burn?
pool.rationale: Alkali injuries raise the pH of tissues, causing saponification of fatty acids in cell membranes, as well as cellular disruption. Acid injuries, on the other hand, lower the pH of tissues and cause denaturing and precipitation of proteins in tissues.  Complement and immunoglobulin deposition is seen in immunobullous diseases, such as mucous membrane pemphigoid. Mast cell degranulation underlies allergic conditions.

pool.q: A patient presents with a history of chemical injury to the eye, followed by recurrent ulcerations of the cornea and decreased vision. On slit-lamp examination, there is corneal neovascularization from the 6 o'clock to the 10 o'clock position and a whorl-like surface irregularity emanating from the limbus with fluorescein staining. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
The answer is limbal stem cell deficiency (LSCD), which can be primary (aniridia, congenital erythrokeratodermia, multiple endocrine deficiency, neurotrophic, or chronic limbitis) or secondary (chemical or thermal injuries, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, ocular cicatricial pemphigoid, chronic contact lens wear, extensive microbial infection, or multiple surgeries or cryotherapies). It consists of a reduced number or an absence of limbal stem cells, leading to conjunctivalization, corneal vascularization, poor epithelial integrity, and chronic inflammation of the ocular surface.
It can be diagnosed clinically or with impression cytology (presence of goblet cells on the cornea). Treatment can be challenging and may include amniotic membrane graft or limbal stem cell transplant (autograft [from the other eye if unilateral] or allograft [from HLA-matched living related donor or from cadaveric eyes]).
Superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis is associated with a superior papillary reaction, injection and thickening of the superior bulbar conjunctiva, hypertrophy of the superior limbus and superior filamentary keratitis. The inferior cornea is not the primary focus of the disease. Peters anomaly is a congenital central or paracentral opacity that is typically avascular and associated with iridocorneal adhesions. Terrien marginal degeneration typically presents in the superonasal quadrant, with progressive circumferential thinning of the peripheral cornea. The corneal epithelium remains intact. Fine pannus transverses the thinned area with a line of lipid deposits at the leading edge of the pannus.

pool.q: A mutation in what gene leads to Reis-Bücklers corneal dystrophy?
pool.rationale:
TGFBI) gene

Mutations in the TGFBI gene may lead to a number of corneal dystrophies, including Reis-Bücklers dystrophy, which is a dystrophy of Bowman layer type 1. Mutations in the gelsolin gene are found in lattice dystrophy type II, while mutations in the UBIAD1 gene are responsible for Schnyder dystrophy. Meesmann dystrophy is caused by mutations in the keratin 3 or keratin 12 gene.

pool.q: What organism is most commonly a component of normal ocular flora?
pool.rationale:
Staphylococcus epidermidis

Staphylococcus epidermidis is a gram-positive bacterium that is a common component of normal ocular flora of the conjunctiva, lid margin, skin, and mucosal surfaces.
Although bacillus cereus, a gram-positive, spore-forming rod, can sometimes be found in normal conjunctiva, it is much less commonly found than staphylococcal species.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a gram-negative bacterium often implicated in contact-lens–related bacterial keratitis.
Clostridium perfringens is a gram-positive, spore-forming anaerobe that can cause food poisoning and gas gangrene.

pool.q: Corneal epithelial microtrauma resulting from the insertion and removal of soft contact lenses seems to play a role in the etiology of what disorder?
pool.rationale: Corneal microabrasions from contact lens wear are one risk factor for infectious keratitis, as most bacteria cannot penetrate through intact epithelium. Staining at 3- and 9'oclock suggests a poor contact lens fit. Peripheral corneal neovascularization is thought to be driven by hypoxia.

pool.q: A 55-year-old woman with a history of multiple episodes of severe eye pain upon awakening presents to a clinic for evaluation. Both eyes have been affected, although not always simultaneously, by her history. What corneal findings are most likely to be present on slit-lamp examination?
pool.rationale:
Recurrent corneal erosions typically occur in eyes that have suffered prior ocular surface trauma, usually an abrading injury with shearing force. Affected individuals often report sudden onset eye pain during the night or upon first awakening, accompanied by redness, photophobia, and tearing. The corneal epithelium may be heaped up and edematous in the setting of an abrasion, or intact at the time of examination. The contralateral eye must be examined to aid in determining the underlying etiology of the recurrent corneal erosion. Unilaterality is suggestive of posttraumatic etiology or pathology related to herpetic keratitis, while bilaterality is more consistent with dystrophic etiology.
In the case example, the bilaterality of the patient's recurrent corneal erosions is most commonly associated with underlying corneal epithelial basement membrane dystrophy (EBMD), which is a bilateral asymmetric condition. Approximately 50% of patients with recurrent corneal erosion are believed to have underlying EBMD, although only 10% of patients with EBMD will develop recurrent corneal erosion. Patterns of corneal epithelial findings evident on slit-lamp examination in EBMD include fingerprint lines, maps, dots, and a bleb pattern (Bron).
Subepithelial infiltrates are most typical of epidemic keratoconjunctivitis. Punctate epithelial erosions are perhaps the most common corneal finding of all, and they are associated with corneal surface dryness from any and all dry eye disease syndromes and tear insufficiency syndromes, but they are not a hallmark of recurrent corneal erosion. Filamentary keratitis is also more characteristically associated with dry eye disease syndromes than with recurrent corneal erosion.

pool.q: In immunocompetent individuals, what is the most common ocular presentation of chronic microsporidial infection?
pool.rationale: Microsporidia is a rare cause of chronic ocular infection in immunocompetent hosts, but when present, it typically manifests as a chronic stromal keratitis, which may be mistaken for herpetic disease. Conjunctivitis and epithelial keratitis are typically seen when microsporidia infects an immunocompromised host, or rarely as a self-limited (but not chronic) infection in immunocompetent hosts. Endotheliitis is not typically seen in chronic microsporidial infection.  Treatments include restoration of immune function and topical fumagillin; in cases of severe stromal thinning, penetrating keratoplasty may be necessary.

pool.q: What condition is characterized by bilateral dysfunctional corneal endothelial cells with epithelial-like behavior?
pool.rationale:
Posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy (PPCD) is characterized by bilateral (can be asymmetric) vesicular or scalloped areas of abnormal endothelium with epithelial characteristics. The abnormal epithelium typically produces progressive or episodic corneal edema and can lead to iridocorneal adhesions, causing corectopia or peripheral anterior synechiae.
Iridocorneal endothelial (ICE) syndrome can mimic all of these features but is characteristically a unilateral condition. Fuchs endothelial dystrophy and congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy are bilateral causes of endothelial dysfunction, but the endothelium does not have the epithelial properties seen in PPMD.

pool.q: Corneal crosslinking has a primary objective of what endpoint?

options.a: reducing corneal curvature in the peripheral cornea
options.d: reducing corneal curvature in the central cornea

pool.rationale:
Corneal crosslinking (CXL) is the first-line treatment to stabilize the cornea. Often, functional visual acuity can be restored with rigid gas-permeable or hybrid contact lenses. The implantation of symmetric or asymmetric intrastromal ring segments to reduce the irregular astigmatism can help in selected cases. Crosslinking has been combined with simultaneous or sequential excimer laser treatment to reduce astigmatism. In extreme cases, corneal transplantation may be required.

CXL is performed to arrest or slow the progression of corneal ectasia in its earlier stages to preserve visual function. The patients will still require glasses or contact lenses; thus, surgeons need to counsel the patients and set realistic expectations regarding the surgical outcomes. CXL is the first-line treatment for mild to moderate corneal ectasia.

pool.q: A woman presents to the emergency department with a 1-day onset of a vesicular rash that respects the right V1 dermatome. If the patient develops ocular involvement, what is the probability that she will have subsequent diminished corneal sensation?
pool.rationale: Ocular involvement occurs in more that 70% of patients with zoster of CN V1, but it may also occur with zoster of CN V2. Corneal manifestations of herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO) include pseudodendrites, which may occur for weeks to months after resolution of skin lesions. Diminished corneal sensation occurs in up to 50% of patients. Neurotrophic keratopathy due to HZO can be very difficult to manage.

pool.q: What conjunctival reaction is most commonly seen with a herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection?
pool.rationale:
Features of HSV blepharoconjunctivitis include:
  • vesicles on skin or eyelid margin
  • raised clear vesicles that progress to blistered, crusted lesions
  • follicular conjunctivitis
  • bulbar conjunctival ulceration
Papillary responses can occur in a variety of conditions, including allergic disease. Pseudomembrane formation can be seen with adenoviral conjunctivitis. Pyogenic granuloma formation can occur after surgery.

pool.q: A patient is referred to an ophthalmologist for treatment of herpes simplex keratoconjunctivitis OS. She has been treated by the referring doctor with 4 weeks of trifluorothymidine, 1 drop to the affected eye 4 times a day (qid), as well as oral acyclovir. She reports little change in her previous symptoms of blurred vision, ocular redness, and irritation. On examination she has mild conjunctival hyperemia and diffuse punctate corneal erosions OS. What is the next appropriate step in this patient's management?

options.b: placement of a bandage contact lens

pool.rationale:
Toxic medication injury of the cornea should be in the differential diagnosis of any patient with diffuse punctate epithelial erosions and a history of prolonged topical medication use (common offending agents include anesthetics, aminoglycosides, antivirals, mitomycin, and drops preserved with benzalkonium chloride). Offending medications may also cause erosive corneal epithelial defects, punctate staining of the conjunctiva, conjunctival injection with a papillary or follicular reaction, and occasionally, mucopurulent discharge that may mimic a bacterial conjunctivitis. Before any additional management is undertaken, first-line therapy includes discontinuation of the offending agent.

pool.q: Several weeks after being successfully treated for herpes zoster ophthalmicus with oral valacyclovir, an elderly patient presents for evaluation of persistent ocular pain on the affected side. On slit-lamp examination, the patient is noted to have an inferior epithelial defect with rolled margins. What diagnostic technique would elucidate the most likely diagnosis in this scenario?
pool.rationale:
The presentation of an inferior epithelial defect with rolled edges in the setting of herpes zoster keratitis is most consistent with a diagnosis of neurotrophic keratopathy, which is due to damaged trigeminal sensation of the cornea. Neurotrophic keratopathy is diagnosed using esthesiometry, a measure of corneal sensation, and is most commonly clinically tested using a cotton-tipped applicator (prior to instillation of topical anesthetic). More quantitative measurements can be obtained using a handheld esthesiometer (eg, Cochet-Bonnet), which is a device containing a retractable nylon monofilament. The length of the filament, correlated to its flex when touching the cornea, is adjusted to the degree of hypoesthesia encountered.
Clinical features of neurotrophic keratopathy include decreased corneal sensation, punctate epithelial erosions (not punctate epithelial keratitis, which would be seen in conditions such as Thygeson superficial punctate keratitis), sterile ulceration (without an infiltrate), and the presence of thickened, rolled, gray, oval-shaped defect borders. Persistent epithelial defects associated with neurotrophic keratopathy tend to be central or paracentral and are often inferior due to the protective effect of the Bell phenomenon on the superior cornea.

pool.q: One week following scleral buckling surgery, a patient presents with a corneal dellen adjacent to the conjunctival wound closure. What is the most appropriate initial management?
pool.rationale:
A corneal dellen is characterized by focal stromal desiccation and thinning, characteristically in the absence of a frank epithelial defect. A dellen most frequently occurs adjacent to an elevated limbal or conjunctival lesion (as may be seen following conjunctival closure or in the setting of a prominent pterygium). The most appropriate first-line management is aggressive lubrication with artificial tears or ointment, with or without pressure patching.
If a positive response is not seen within 1 to 2 days, surgical revision or resection of the offending tissue should be considered. Tarsorrhaphy and amniotic membrane grafting play a role in the treatment of non-healing epithelial defects and corneal ulcers, but typically are not first-line treatment for a corneal dellen.

pool.q: A young child with a new diagnosis of xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) is referred for ocular examination. After counseling the child's parents on sun protection and symptoms of dry eye, the ophthalmologist explains the need for frequent follow-up to monitor for the development of what condition?
pool.rationale: XP is an autosomal recessive disease characterized by the inability to repair DNA damaged by ultraviolet light. Commonly associated ocular conditions are keratoconjunctivitis sicca, exposure keratitis, pinguecula, and pterygia. Ocular neoplasms occur in 11% of patients and require frequent monitoring. These include squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma, and melanoma both on the ocular surface and the eyelids. XP is not associated with solar retinopathy, and there is no strong association between early cataract formation and XP.

pool.q: What primary intraocular malignancy would be considered acceptable in a potential donor cornea?
pool.rationale:
The Eye Bank Association of America and the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) have developed extensive criteria for screening donor corneas prior to distribution to avoid transmissible infections and other conditions. Intraocular neoplasms contraindicating donor cornea use include retinoblastoma, disseminated lymphoma, adenocarcinoma, and any anterior segment malignancy. Eyes with localized posterior choroidal melanoma are considered acceptable, although some medical eye bank directors decline their use.

(A figure accompanies this rationale on the section page.)

pool.q: What condition is characterized by a chronic, painful ulceration of the peripheral corneal stroma and epithelium with severe corneal thinning?
pool.rationale: Mooren ulcer is a chronic, progressive painful idiopathic ulceration of the peripheral cornea. The epithelium is affected, and there can be severe peripheral corneal thinning and perforation. Staphylococcal marginal keratitis has a more indolent course, and may be characterized by intact epithelium, mild to moderate pain, and little to no corneal stromal thinning. Terrien marginal degeneration and senile furrow degeneration are nonpainful, slowly progressive degenerations of the cornea.

pool.q: A 73-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a corneal abnormality. The patient underwent trabeculectomy 1 week prior. On examination, there is an elevated bleb superiorly. There is the appearance of thinning and pooling of fluorescein in the corneal periphery adjacent to the bleb. What is the best treatment plan for this patient?

options.c: frequent topical, fortified vancomycin and tobramycin

pool.rationale: Dellen are saucerlike depressions in the corneal surface due to focal stromal dehydration. They often occur at or near the limbus, adjacent to conjunctival surface elevations. There is pooling of fluorescein with minimal staining. Since they are not infectious in nature, topical antibiotics such as fluoroquinolones, vancomycin, or tobramycin will not be effective. A dellen would not be an indication for bleb revision. Patching and frequent lubrication will be most effective in rehydrating the corneal stroma and resolving the dellen.

pool.q: For a 36-year-old woman with a 20-year history of soft contact lens wear and 270 degrees of bilateral, diffuse whorled corneal epithelium, and 3 mm of peripheral neovascularization, what is the most appropriate initial management?

options.b: Place bilateral large-diameter soft bandage contact lenses.

pool.rationale:
The presentation is consistent with severe limbal stem cell deficiency (LSCD) in a young patient with extensive history of contact lens wear. Women, especially long-term soft contact lens wearers, are the most susceptible to developing LSCD. The most important initial intervention is to remove any ongoing toxic insult to the limbal stem cells; for the patient in this scenario, complete cessation of contact lens wear is necessary.
Bandage soft contact lenses may artificially relieve some of the patient's discomfort, but they are not indicated in this case, because they can worsen the LSCD. Topical steroids may be useful adjunctive measures to long-term management of LSCD, but they are not as important as stopping contact lens wear. Limbal transplantation can sometimes be necessary in severe cases, but it is not appropriate initial treatment.

pool.q: What test is important to perform in a patient with a persistent corneal epithelial defect?
pool.rationale:
A common cause of persistent epithelial defects is neurotrophic keratopathy, which can be seen in the setting of herpes simplex virus, herpes zoster virus, and diabetes. As such, it is important to check corneal sensation, or corneal esthesiometry, in these patients. While a wisp of cotton from a cotton applicator is most commonly used for this purpose, handheld esthesiometers can better quantify cornea sensation.

pool.q: What anatomic distribution of acquired noncystic, flat, patchy or diffuse brown pigmentation of the conjunctiva is most associated with possible progression to conjunctival melanoma?

Your diagnosis will likely be complexion-associated melanosis (CAM) which is usually bilateral and symmetric and carries very little risk of progression to melanoma. CAM usually is in the setting of a darker skin; however it can develop in all races (5% of whites). Larger size (3 clock-hours or more) also may predict progression to melanoma. Thus, involvement of more than 2 clock-hours of conjunctiva is a reason to excise the lesion to send to pathology for diagnosis.
Of note, other worrisome findings include enlargement, a nodular appearance, feeder vessels, and thickening.
Most malignant melanoma of the conjunctiva arise from PAM (70%). 5% arise from nevi and 25% arise de novo. Any pigmented lesion on the palpebral conjunctiva, cornea or in the fornix should be biopsied.

Again, bilateral pigmentation is more commonly associated with CAM, which, even with palpebral conjunctival involvement, is still very unlikely to progress to melanoma.

pool.q: What is the source for the generation of singlet oxygen and superoxide anion-free oxygen radicals in collagen crosslinking procedures?

pool.q: In a patient with herpes zoster ophthalmicus, what clinical finding may warrant performing a tarsorrhaphy?

pool.q: What are typical skin findings seen in rosacea?

options.a: vesicles with ulceration, weeping, and scarring
options.c: shiny, white-yellow papule with central umbilication

Rosacea is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction that is more common in fair-skinned individuals aged 30-60 years. Patients have cutaneous sebaceous gland dysfunction that causes erythema, pustules, papules, and telangiectasia of the facial skin. Patients can develop a malar rash. Rhinophyma (large, bulb-shaped, red-colored nose) occurs later in the disease course. More than 50% of patients will have ocular involvement, which can include blepharitis, chalazion, keratoconjunctivitis sicca, and keratitis. The condition may be exacerbated by ultraviolet light, alcohol, and caffeine. Treatment options include oral tetracycline/doxycycline, oral flaxseed oil and omega-3 fatty acids, and topical metronidazole to facial skin. Ocular involvement may be treated with eyelid hygiene, topical antibiotic ointments/gels, and artificial tears.
Erythematous scaling lesions occur with contact dermatitis. Other manifestations may include erythema, edema, and itchy periorbital skin. This condition may occur around the eyes secondary to makeup, soaps, or eye drops.

The virus can also cause a follicular conjunctivitis and punctate keratitis. Occasionally, basal cell carcinoma on the lid may have a central ulceration that may mimic a molluscum lesion.

If the reactivation occurs in V1 (nasociliary nerve), patients are most likely to have ocular manifestation of the virus. pool.q: What refractive procedure may be appropriate for the correction of refractive error in a patient with keratoconus?

LASIK and PRK are contraindicated in patients with manifest or forme fruste keratoconus. The safety and efficacy of surface ablation, combined with or performed after collagen cross-linking, is under investigation and may be a viable alternative therapeutic modality for these patients.
Although some early case reports have suggested that combining CCL treatments with PRK may offer some benefit to keratoconus patients, the clinical experience remains preliminary.

pool.q: What is a risk factor for epithelial basement membrane dystrophy (EBMD)?

pool.q: While on an ophthalmology mission trip, the clinician examines a 12-year-old boy who reports chronic vision loss in the right eye. pool.q: What diagnostic technique provides the most direct assessment of the corneal endothelium?
pool.rationale: Specular microscopy is a diagnostic technique that provides direct, objective assessment of corneal endothelial health. Density, coefficient of variation (standard deviation of mean cell area divided by mean cell area), and percentage of hexagonal cells are all objective measures of endothelial cell health provided by specular microscopy. Endothelial cell density < 1000 cells/mm2, high polymegethism (variability of individual cell areas) as indicated by coefficient of variation > 0.40, and high pleomorphism (variability of individual cell shape) as indicated by percentage of nonhexagonal cells > 50% are all factors associated with corneal decompensation following cataract surgery. Ultrasound pachymetry indirectly assesses endothelial function by measuring central corneal thickness, which is a function of corneal hydration, and thus a proxy of endothelial pump function. A central corneal thickness measurement of 640 µm also suggests higher risk of corneal decompensation following cataract surgery. Ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM) and anterior segment optical coherence tomography both provide high resolution images of the anterior segment, but do not generate indicators of endothelial health.

pool.q: Nonnutrient agar with an Escherichia coli overlay is useful for culturing what organism?
pool.rationale:
Acanthamoeba

This question is most relevant for corneal ulcers. It is important to determine the etiology of a corneal ulcer with a corneal culture when:
  • it is large or sight-threatening
  • an atypical organism is suspected
  • therapy is not working

When collecting a specimen for Chlamydia testing, one should use Chlamydial transport medium, and it is recommended that a Dacron swab is used to collect the specimen. pool.q: What is the most appropriate long-term treatment of atopic dermatitis and associated atopic keratoconjunctivitis uncontrolled by topical therapies?
pool.rationale:

It involves a type IV hypersensitivity reaction, increased immunoglobulin E hypersensitivity, increased histamine released from mast cells and basophils, and impaired cell-mediated immunity. Treatment includes identifying and minimizing allergens in the environment and in foods. Moisturizing lotions and petrolatum gels can be useful for skin hydration. Acute lesions can be controlled with a topical corticosteroid cream or ointment (eg, clobetasone butyrate 0.05%), but to avoid skin thinning and ocular complications of steroids, long-term use of such medications is strongly discouraged.
Cyclosporine is the only drug approved by the US Food and Drug Administration to treat atopic dermatitis; it remains first line and is the most appropriate treatment. Topical and oral T-cell inhibitors (eg, tacrolimus) have been found effective and have fewer adverse effects than corticosteroids, so they are used in patients with chronic and severe disease. Oral antipruritic agents such as antihistamines and mast-cell stabilizers can alleviate itching, but can exacerbate dry eye with their anticholinergic activity. Oral doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine are not used in the treatment of atopic dermatitis or atopic keratoconjunctivitis.

As a result, amniotic membrane grafts are often performed early in the disease course.

pool.q: Subtle abnormalities in posterior corneal curvature are best evaluated by what diagnostic tool?

pool.q: A 35-year-old woman wearing toric soft contact lenses desires laser refractive surgery. Her topography reveals irregular astigmatism and peripheral corneal thinning inferiorly 1-2 mm from the limbus. Her central corneal thickness is normal. Her history is remarkable for long-standing atopic disease. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Pellucid marginal degeneration, keratoconus, and keratoglobus are all bilateral corneal ectatic disorders with corneal thinning.
In pellucid marginal degeneration, the stromal thinning is peripheral, typically seen inferiorly 1 to 2 mm from the limbus. In contrast to keratoconus, maximal corneal protrusion occurs superior to, rather than within, the area of thinning. Corneal topography maps show a typical "crab-claw" appearance corresponding to inferior steepening.
The protrusion of the cornea in keratoconus is central and the apex of the cone is usually centered just below the visual axis. The area of maximal protrusion occurs in the area of maximal thinning.
Patients with keratoglobus have a globular protrusion of the cornea from generalized thinning, most marked in the periphery. The cornea has a normal or slightly increased diameter.
Patients with corneal ectatic disorders are poor candidates for refractive surgery because of the risk of postoperative progressive ectasia.
Corneal warpage refers to irregular astigmatism induced by contact lens wear. There is no corneal thinning present. It occurs most commonly with rigid gas permeable lenses, but it can be seen with soft contact lenses. Corneal warpage resolves when contact lens wear is discontinued and can be followed until refraction and topography stabilize.

pool.q: Following unilateral chemical corneal burn with complete conjunctivalization of the cornea, what surgical option is most likely to result in improvement?

If total loss of limbal stem cells occurs bilaterally, options include harvesting stem cells from a living related donor (limbal stem cell allograft) or from an eye bank donor cornea (keratolimbal allograft). pool.q: Patients with atopic keratoconjunctivitis are particularly susceptible to what type of infection?

pool.q: What is the most appropriate initial treatment of the ocular complications of Stevens-Johnson syndrome?

In cases of severe ocular surface involvement, amniotic membrane transplantation over the entire ocular surface can have long-term benefit.

pool.q: Why are pediatric corneal transplants more likely to fail than corneal transplants in adults?

options.a: There is a higher incidence of preexisting corneal neovascularization in pediatrics.
options.b: Sutures must stay in longer after a pediatric corneal transplant.
options.c: Pediatric corneal transplants take longer to re-epithelialize.
options.d: Resultant astigmatism is higher after pediatric corneal transplant.

pool.rationale:
Coexisting ocular abnormalities do occur in many adults who need corneal transplants (eg, glaucoma patients who may have shunt devices) and could compromise the integrity and survival of the graft. However, relatively speaking, most adult cases requiring corneal transplants are due to Fuchs dystrophy, pseudophakic bullous keratopathy (and the energy to phacoemulsify the lens and damage the endothelium would not be required again or threaten the new graft), and corneal scarring. Although repeat grafts often have the disadvantage of resulting in corneal neovascularization of the host cornea bed in adults, this is less common with the first graft.
In contrast, many pediatric cases requiring corneal transplant are for conditions such as Peters anomaly, which often have anterior segment findings including adhesions between surrounding structures (cornea, iris, lens), glaucoma, and untreated cataract, all of which make the surgical procedure longer, more extensive, and at higher risk for corneal graft failure due to increased handling of the tissue. Additionally, corneal neovascularization of the host bed is more common in pediatrics, and this is more likely to bring immune cells to the graft, which would lead to rejection.
Due to young age and lack of major medical comorbidities in most cases, re-epithelialization after a corneal transplant in a child is actually more likely to occur quickly, protecting the cornea from immune attack.
Pediatric patients have a higher risk of early loosening of sutures after penetrating keratoplasty. The sutures do not have to stay in longer in children; however, rapid neovascularization, especially along sutures, is particularly prevalent in corneal grafts in children under 2 years of age and can lead to rejection. As such, regular examinations under anesthesia are needed, with early suture removal and protection from self-induced trauma.
Astigmatism is not a reason for corneal transplant rejection. However, due to the high risk of amblyopia due to astigmatism in infants and young children, it is imperative to have the child fitted for a contact lens either at the time of surgery or shortly thereafter, and to use ocular occlusive therapy aggressively to prevent amblyopia.

pool.q: Tarsorrhaphy is indicated as a treatment for what type of corneal ulcer?
pool.rationale:
Common indications for tarsorrhaphy include severe, recalcitrant keratopathy, persistent epithelial defect, or corneal thinning resulting from (1) neurogenic exposure keratopathy (cranial nerve [CN] VII palsy), (2) neurotrophic corneal ulceration (CN V deficit, herpes simplex virus [HSV] or varicella zoster virus [VZV] keratitis), (3) eyelid abnormalities, or (4) exposure (thyroid eye disease). Active microbial (bacterial or fungal) keratitis is a contraindication to tarsorrhaphy.
In neurotrophic ulcer, there is damage to the trigeminal nerve, leading to reduced corneal sensation, spontaneous epithelial breakdown, and poor healing. Tarsorrhaphy enhances healing by reducing exposure. Autoimmune corneal ulcer, or peripheral ulcerative keratitis, occurs as white blood cells infiltrate the peripheral cornea and often needs systemic immunosuppression as a treatment, along with topical collagenase inhibitors such as N-acetylcysteine.

pool.q: What characteristic conjunctival finding is commonly seen in a patient presenting with herpes simplex virus (HSV) keratitis?

Thus, HSV infection would lead to a follicular conjunctivitis. pool.q: In the United States, what is an acceptable donor cornea preservation time for corneal transplantation of corneas stored in Optisol?

Primary closure with nylon sutures is generally not feasible, especially in the setting of acute infectious keratitis in which the surrounding tissue is also likely necrotic. pool.q: A history of what refractive therapy precludes a cornea from use as penetrating keratoplasty tissue?

  • Death of unknown cause
  • Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, or family member with Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
  • Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis
  • Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy
  • Congenital rubella
  • Down syndrome
  • Reye syndrome

  • Active septicemia (bacteremia, fungemia, viremia)
  • Active bacterial or fungal endocarditis
  • Active viral hepatitis
  • Rabies
  • Active and intrinsic eye disease (intraocular malignant tumors, infections, inflammatory diseases)
  • Leukemias and lymphomas

pool.q: Superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis causes what type of conjunctival reaction?
pool.rationale:
Superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis is a chronic, recurrent condition of ocular irritation and redness that predominantly affects the superior cornea and conjunctiva. The superior bulbar conjunctiva can be injected and thickened, while a fine papillary reaction is often seen on the superior tarsal conjunctiva. Papillae are dilated vessels with surrounding edema and inflammatory cells producing raised elevations of the conjunctival epithelium. Papillary reactions are also seen in conditions such as allergic conjunctivitis and bacterial conjunctivitis, and in chronic contact lens wear.
In a follicular reaction, clusters of conjunctival lymphocytes become enlarged. Vessels surround the raised surface of follicles but are not prominent within the follicle. Follicular reactions are seen in conditions such as viral conjunctivitis, molluscum contagiosum, and chlamydial conjunctivitis.

pool.q: A 42-year-old man presents with severe right eye pain that began upon awakening this morning. Two weeks ago, he sustained an injury to the eye from a fingernail and was treated for a corneal abrasion. This is his second recurrence of pain since the initial injury. He denies additional trauma. What treatment would be the most appropriate next step to prevent recurrence of his condition?
pool.rationale:
This patient is presenting with recurrent corneal erosions following trauma. Hypertonic saline ointment can be helpful for this condition by facilitating epithelial adherence through creation of an osmotic gradient, drawing fluid from epithelial cells.
Although cyclopentolate can be utilized in the acute phase to reduce pain, it would have no role in preventing recurrence of this condition.
Surgical therapy with either anterior stromal puncture or phototherapeutic keratectomy should be reserved for patients with recurrent corneal erosions that have not responded to medical treatment.
