pool.q: What should adult-onset varicella-zoster virus epithelial keratitis be treated with?
pool.rationale:
Epithelial keratitis indicates the presence of live, replicating varicella-zoster virus within the corneal epithelium. Oral antiviral therapy with acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir is the preferred treatment for live, replicating zoster virus.
Topical medication such as trifluridine may be effective but has the disadvantage of only treating the ocular surface and conveying some degree of toxicity, which can limit or delay epithelial healing. Topical antivirals should be reserved for recurrent epithelial lesions or rare cases with contraindications to systemic therapy. Artificial tears provide lubrication, which aids in healing after ocular surface breakdown but does not inhibit replicating varicella-zoster virus. Intravitreal ganciclovir is an effective treatment for intraocular involvement of varicella zoster but is not effective in treating virus on the ocular surface.

pool.q: What corneal ectasia is characteristically bilateral, noninflammatory, not hereditary, and typically present at birth?

Unlike keratoconus or pellucid marginal degeneration, keratoglobus is normally present at birth. Posterior keratoconus is a central or paracentral indentation of the posterior cornea that is present at birth and is classified as a congenital anomaly. Posterior keratoconus is most frequently unilateral and sporadic, although an autosomal recessive form of disease with bilateral corneal findings has been described that is also associated with other findings such as short stature, cleft lip and palate, vertebral anomalies, and intellectual disability.

options.d: granular epithelial lesions with minimal conjunctival injection

pool.q: What finding is specific for blepharitis caused by staphylococcus?
pool.rationale:
Blepharitis is an inflammation of the eyelid margins that causes ocular irritation. The most common cause of blepharitis is a staphylococcus infection, which typically presents with hard, brittle fibrinous scales and hard, matted crusts surrounding individual cilia (collarettes) on the anterior eyelid margin. The irritation from the infection can lead to eyelid ulceration, corneal vascularization, marginal infiltrates, or punctate erosions. Treatment modalities to decrease bacterial load and reduce inflammation include lid hygiene, lubrication, antibiotic ointment or pills, or anti-inflammatory drops.
Seborrheic blepharitis patients have increased oil secretion, with greasy scales along the lashes. Cylindrical sleeves around the lash bases occur in patients with Demodex colonization. Meibomian gland inspissations occur in posterior blepharitis or meibomian gland dysfunction. Rapid tear breakup is commonly found in patients with meibomian gland dysfunction. The tear breakup time will also be affected in aqueous tear deficiency (Sjögren and non-Sjögren etiologies).

pool.q: What mucopolysaccharidosis (MPS) has an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern?

pool.q: What is the most typical appearance of corneal intraepithelial neoplasia?

options.a: single, dense corneal opacity with fluorescein uptake
options.b: translucent gray epithelial sheet with fimbriated margins
options.c: multifocal white opacities in a circinate pattern

Corneal intraepithelial neoplasia typically manifests as a translucent, sometimes granular, gray epithelial sheet that is based at the limbus and extends onto the cornea. The edges have characteristic fimbriated margins and pseudopodia-like extensions.

pool.q: A patient with dry age-related macular degeneration presents with new-onset decreased vision. The ophthalmologist orders fluorescein angiography. A few minutes later, the patient reports that he feels short of breath and starts wheezing. This is an example of what type of hypersensitivity?
pool.rationale:
Type I hypersensitivity is triggered by the activation of IgE. Presumably, the IgE producing B lymphocytes were "primed" by prior exposure to the antigen (in this case, fluorescein). The Fc portion of the IgE antibody binds to mast cells, causing them to degranulate and release interleukins and cytokines. This happens within several minutes of re-exposure. These inflammatory mediators can cause blood vessel dilation and massive edema, leading to reactions ranging from hives, urticarial, laryngeal edema, to ultimately, anaphylaxis.
Type II hypersensitivity is defined as a hypersensitivity reaction secondary to antibodies that are directly cytotoxic against human tissues. Examples of type II hypersensitivity include Goodpasture syndrome and cicatricial pemphigoid.
Type III hypersensitivity is defined as a hypersensitivity secondary to antibody-antigen immune complex reactions. Examples of type III hypersensitivity include systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis,
Type IV hypersensitivity is a delayed cell-mediated reaction. T lymphocytes are responsible for this hypersensitivity. Examples of type IV hypersensitivity include contact dermatitis, staph marginal keratitis, and purified protein derivative (PPD) placement.

pool.q: What corneal disorder is most amenable to a treatment by superficial keratectomy alone?

Contraindications for the procedure include corneal dystrophies or degenerations producing visual loss via stromal opacification.

pool.q: What surgical procedure is typically used to treat total unilateral limbal stem cell deficiency?

options.b: limbal stem cell transplant from eye bank donor cornea
options.c: transplant of stem cells cultured from oral mucosa
options.d: limbal stem cell transplant from the fellow eye

If total unilateral limbal stem cell deficiency occurs, an autograft of limbal epithelium from the fellow eye is most commonly used.

pool.q: What histopathologic characteristic is associated most with melanoma transformation in primary acquired melanosis?

pool.q: What is the appropriate adjunctive therapy for perilimbal conjunctival melanoma with suspected corneal epithelial involvement?

options.c: external beam radiation focused on the corneal epithelium

Conjunctival melanoma is associated with a very high rate of local recurrence (up to 50%). In cases with perilimbal involvement and possible corneal epithelial extension, adjuvant local therapy should be strongly considered. Absolute alcohol epitheliectomy is one option to treat the epithelium selectively.
Tectonic penetrating keratoplasty is unwarranted, because the disease is confined the superficial cornea. External beam radiation cannot be targeted to the corneal epithelium specifically and may result in significant local complications. Observation alone is not recommended, based on the high-risk nature of these neoplasms.

pool.q: Meretoja syndrome (systemic amyloidosis associated with lattice corneal dystrophy) is found in patients who have a gene mutation that results in what abnormal protein product?

Gelsolin type (type 2) lattice corneal dystrophy is associated with Meretoja syndrome (systemic amyloidosis with lattice dystrophy). Since Meretoja syndrome is a systemic syndrome, it is not classified as a corneal dystrophy by the International Committee for the Classification of Corneal Dystrophies (IC3D).

pool.q: What location of conjunctival melanoma is associated with the best long-term prognosis?

pool.q: What intervention can help prevent pupillary block glaucoma after Descemet stripping automated endothelial keratoplasty (DSAEK)?

pool.rationale:
In DSAEK (also referred to as DSEK), air is injected into the anterior chamber in order to promote graft attachment to the host cornea. If the air bubble obstructs aqueous flow through the pupil, acute pupillary block angle closure can occur. Interventions that prevent this complication include pharmacologic mydriasis, inferior peripheral iridectomy, and/or avoiding a large air bubble that might cover the pupil.
Face-down or prone positioning and pharmacologic miosis should be avoided because they increase the risk of pupillary obstruction by the air bubble. Ocular hypotensive agents may lower the intraocular pressure (IOP) if it is elevated post-DSEK, but they would not correct the underlying issue of pupillary block.

pool.q: A number of factors actively contribute to immune tolerance of corneal grafts. How does the cornea actively prevent rejection of corneal transplants?

options.a: presence of major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II antigen-presenting cells
options.b: presence of pro-inflammatory cytokines in the aqueous humor
options.c: increased lymphatic channels in graft bed
options.d: triggering apoptosis through upregulation of Fas ligand

pool.rationale:
Many factors actively contribute to "immunologic privilege" of transplanted corneal tissue, facilitating graft survival. These factors include:
  • absence of blood or lymphatic channels in graft and graft bed
  • absence of MHC class II antigen-presenting cells (APCs) in graft
  • reduced expression of MHC-encoded alloantigens on graft cells
  • increased expression of Fas ligand, which stimulates apoptosis of killer T cells
  • immunosuppressive cytokines in aqueous humor, including TGF-β2, vasoactive intestinal peptide, and α-melanocyte-stimulating hormone
  • development of suppressor T cells from aqueous humor antigens

pool.q: What is the primary cause of exposure keratopathy in patients with Parkinson disease?
pool.rationale:
The major cause of exposure keratopathy in patients with Parkinson disease is poor blink frequency. Patients may also suffer from reduced tear production as a result of anti-Parkinson medications. Parkinson is a degenerative neurologic condition.
Although progressive facial paralysis does occur, the mechanism of exposure is not cicatricial ectropion. Proptosis and upper-eyelid retraction are features of thyroid eye disease (TED), not Parkinson disease.

pool.q: What type of device is best for detecting abnormalities in posterior corneal curvature?
pool.rationale: Scheimpflug-based imaging platforms (eg, Pentacam, Orbscan) are the most commonly employed devices for mapping posterior corneal curvature. These devices employ a scanning beam that "slices" through the cornea and generates maps based on the anterior-posterior dimensions of the cornea. Placido disk and videokeratoscopic imaging devices only provide information about the anterior surface (both devices use surface reflections and hence are unable to assess to the posterior cornea). Ultrasonic pachymetry can measure and detect areas of relative thickness disparity, but it is not typically employed to assess and monitor posterior corneal curvature.

pool.q: Under physiologic conditions, what interface provides the majority of refractive power for the human eye?
pool.rationale: Owing to both the curvature as well as the large difference in index of refraction, the air to tear film interface provides the majority of refractive power for the normal human eye. As such, disorders that alter the corneal surface or tear film may produce significant visual aberrations, whereas a similar degree of pathology in the posterior cornea typically results in far fewer visual symptoms. Although the corneal endothelium to aqueous and aqueous to lens capsule transitions both contribute to the total refraction, the effect is greatly reduced by the relatively similar indices of refraction to the aqueous. Very little refraction takes places between the tear film and corneal epithelium, owing to the similar curvatures and indices of refraction.

pool.q: What condition is most closely associated with papillary conjunctivitis?
pool.rationale:
Patients with atopic keratoconjunctivitis show signs of type I immediate hypersensitivity, which manifests as a papillary conjunctivitis.
In contrast, adult inclusion, herpes simplex, and molluscum contagiosum typically demonstrate follicular conjunctivitis.

pool.q: In what clinical setting should empiric systemic antibiotics be considered to treat conjunctivitis?

options.b: serous conjunctivitis following a recent upper respiratory tract infection
options.c: chronic intermittent conjunctivitis in a patient with sleep apnea
options.d: giant papillary conjunctivitis in the setting of soft contact lens wear

pool.rationale:
Generally speaking, conjunctivitis does not require systemic therapy. Indications for initiating systemic antibiotic therapy in the setting of conjunctivitis include acute purulent conjunctivitis with pharyngitis, conjunctivitis with concurrent otitis media, Haemophilus conjunctivitis in children, and culture-proven cases of chlamydial or gonococcal etiology.
Chronic intermittent conjunctivitis in a patient with sleep apnea should prompt the examiner to look for signs of floppy eyelid syndrome.
Giant papillary conjunctivitis caused by soft contact lens wear can be managed with topical anti-inflammatory medications or changing the composition of the contact lens material.
Serous conjunctivitis in the setting of a recent upper respiratory tract infection is likely to be viral in origin.

pool.q: What lens finding is most characteristic in a patient with atopic keratoconjunctivitis?
pool.rationale:
Anterior subcapsular cataracts are most commonly seen in patients with chronic atopic keratoconjunctivitis. Posterior polar cataracts are typically congenital and may be bilateral (often autosomal dominant inheritance) or unilateral (sporadic).
Anterior lenticonus is a very rare malformation of the anterior capsule that can be seen in patients with Alport syndrome (nephrotic hematuria and deafness), Lowe syndrome (oculocerebral renal syndrome), and Waardenburg syndrome (deafness and partial albinism). Posterior lenticonus may be associated with microcornea, hyperglycinuria, Duane syndrome, anterior lentiplanus, and MPPC (microcornea, posterior megalolenticonus, persistent fetal vasculature, coloboma).

pool.q: What is a contraindication to crosslinking in moderate keratoconus?

options.a: previous laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) treatment

pool.rationale:
Having a history of neurotrophic keratopathy may result in poor epithelial healing. Collagen crosslinking utilizes vitamin B2 (riboflavin) and ultraviolet A (UVA) light to strengthen the cornea and to stabilize the corneal curvature. The treatment leads to new physical crosslinks of the corneal collagen fibers. The procedure involves removing the corneal epithelium, placing frequent topical riboflavin drops, and exposing the cornea to UVA light for approximately 30 minutes. The effects take up to 6 months to peak. Complications can include corneal haze, decreased corneal sensitivity, sterile or microbial keratitis, corneal scarring, persistent corneal edema, and decreased vision.
Crosslinking is recommended in patients with progressive disease, especially in adolescents. Although crosslinking may not be as effective in patients post LASIK treatment or with severe disease, it is not contraindicated. It may be performed in concert with intrastromal ring insertion. It is currently contraindicated in concurrent ocular infection, severe corneal scarring, past history of poor epithelial wound healing, history of autoimmune diseases, pregnancy, and history of neurotrophic keratopathy. Hydrops occurs due to a tear in Descemet membrane, usually late in the course of keratoconus, and although following resolution with improvement in corneal edema, there is some stromal scarring, it is not an absolute contraindication to crosslinking.

pool.q: An obese 48-year-old man presents with irritation that is greater in his right eye than his left eye. There is scant discharge in both eyes. He states his symptoms are worse in the morning upon awakening. There is some punctate corneal staining and some corneal vascularization. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
This clinical presentation is typical for floppy eyelid syndrome. Patients will demonstrate lid laxity, more commonly of upper eyelids than the lower eyelids. Disease can be unilateral or asymmetric, and patients can present with mild corneal epitheliopathy and papillae on upper lids. The syndrome is frequently seen in obese patients.
Vernal conjunctivitis does not present with lid laxity; it is a type of allergic conjunctivitis that presents with burning and itching. It has 2 forms, palpebral and limbal, and occasionally a combination of the 2 types.
Giant papillary conjunctivitis (GPC) is an allergic condition of the eyes seen most commonly in contact lens wearers. The upper lids show the formation of large papillae greater than .3 mm.
Thygeson superficial punctate keratitis is a condition marked by elevated corneal opacities, typically in both eyes, without inflammation; it tends to be chronic.

pool.q: For what condition is bilateral presentation of viral keratitis common?
pool.rationale: Due to its virulence, epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (adenovirus serotypes 8, 19, 37; subgroup D) typically presents with bilateral corneal involvement that can include punctate epithelial keratitis associated with the severe follicular conjunctivitis. Herpes simplex, herpes zoster, and molluscum contagiosum typically present unilaterally or, in the case of molluscum, in localized clusters.

pool.q: What is the most common cause of conjunctival concretions?

options.d: prior ocular surgery and dry eye

pool.rationale: Concretions are epithelial inclusion cysts filled with epithelial and keratin debris. Yellow-white deposits are sometimes found in the palpebral conjunctiva of patients who are elderly or who have chronic conjunctivitis. They are not a result of hypercalcemia, sun exposure, trachoma, rubbing, surgery, or dry eyes. They are usually asymptomatic, but they can be removed under topical anesthesia if they cause a foreign-body sensation.

pool.q: When evaluating a potential donor cornea for transplantation, a documented history of what procedure is an absolute contraindication for use in penetrating keratoplasty?
pool.rationale:
For the purpose of evaluating prospective corneal donor tissue, previous refractive surgery (LASIK, photorefractive keratectomy [PRK] and radial keratotomy [RK]) is an absolute contraindication for use in penetrating keratoplasty. LASIK and PRK, are, however, acceptable for use with endothelial keratoplasty (DSAEK or DMEK).
Intraocular surgery, including cataract surgery and vitreoretinal surgery, is a relative contraindication to corneal transplantation, but is acceptable if the endothelial cell density is normal and any surgical scars are outside of the area of trephination. Previous extraocular muscle surgery does not impact cornea transplantation eligibility.

pool.q: Reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus (VZV) most commonly involves what cranial nerve?
pool.rationale: The fifth cranial nerve (CN V) is the cranial nerve most frequently affected by reactivation of latent varicella zoster, but CN V is also the most commonly inoculated nerve. Varicella zoster can be acquired as chickenpox or shingles either through direct contact with cutaneous lesions or by aerosolized respiratory droplets. The cornea and conjunctiva are moist, wet surfaces at risk of infection if inoculated by VZV. Varicella rarely infects cranial nerves II, III, or VII, so reactivation in those nerves is less likely.

pool.q: A 58-year-old obese man presents with chronic ocular irritation and inflammation. On examination, there is significant eyelid laxity, and the upper tarsus everts with minimal upward force. What systemic workup is indicated?
pool.rationale:
Floppy eyelid syndrome is characterized by chronic ocular irritation, inflammation, and eyelid laxity. Upper eyelid eversion occurs with minimal upward force. It is most frequently seen in obese patients and is associated with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), which can be diagnosed with a sleep study. Floppy eyelid syndrome is not associated with abnormal brain imaging, abnormal buccal mucosa, or thyroid abnormalities.
In addition to floppy eyelid syndrome, OSA is also a risk factor for non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) and idiopathic intracranial hypertension. Less clear are the associations between OSA and glaucoma, central serous chorioretinopathy, retinal vein occlusion and diabetic maculopathy.

pool.q: What form of scleritis is most commonly associated with increased ocular and systemic morbidity?
pool.rationale:
Scleritis is often associated with systemic disease, especially rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, seronegative spondyloarthropathies, polyarteritis nodosa, and giant cell arteritis. Infectious and metabolic causes (such as gout) should also be considered in the differential diagnosis.
Necrotizing scleritis is the most destructive form of scleritis and can cause either ocular or systemic complications in up to 60% of affected patients. It is further subdivided into necrotizing scleritis with or without inflammation.

pool.q: What is a common clinical finding in persistent corneal epithelial defects?
pool.rationale: Persistent corneal epithelial defects are areas of chronic nonhealing epithelium. They frequently have elevated, rounded edges or scalloped borders and are round or oval in shape. A dendritiform shape is uncharacteristic and should prompt further evaluation for herpetic keratitis. The most common location for a persistent epithelial defect is inferior or inferonasal as a result of the protective effect of Bell phenomenon on the superior cornea. Persistent epithelial defects are commonly seen in neurotrophic keratopathy, so corneal hypoesthesia or anesthesia is often present.

pool.q: What is the most appropriate surgical therapy for a patient with painful band keratopathy?
pool.rationale:
EDTA chelation is a rapid and effective method for removing calcium from the anterior corneal stroma.
Anterior stromal micropuncture is a treatment that can be used for recurrent corneal erosions due to previous trauma or anterior basement membrane dystrophy (ABMD), but it has no role in the management of band keratopathy.
Deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty is unnecessarily invasive for the treatment of band keratopathy, which is limited to the anterior stroma and more effectively treated with EDTA chelation.
LASIK is not an appropriate treatment for band keratopathy.

pool.q: On slit-lamp examination, a patient is found to have an elevated pterygium with an adjacent area of corneal thinning. The epithelium is intact. What is the best treatment option for the corneal thinning?
pool.rationale: The answer is lubrication. The case is describing a dellen at the leading edge of an elevated pterygium. A dellen occurs when there is focal thinning from dehydration of the stroma due to adjacent elevation (pinguecula, pterygium, filtering bleb) in the area. There are 2 appropriate treatment options for this patient. The first step should be to try aggressive lubrication. If this does not completely alleviate the condition, surgical excision of the pterygium should be considered. Pterygium excision will restore the normal tear film to this area and prevent further formation of the dellen. Since the dellen is neither an inflammatory nor infectious process, corticosteroids and topical antibiotics would not help treat the condition. A penetrating keratoplasty is not necessary for this condition.

pool.q: What surgical intervention can be performed to alleviate chronic pain associated with a chronic sterile corneal ulcer in an eye with poor vision potential?
pool.rationale: Conjunctival flap surgery (Gundersen flap) is an effective procedure to control chronic pain in the setting of a non-healing corneal defect. Although retrobulbar alcohol injection can be used for pain relief, it would not be a suitable choice in the setting of a chronic epithelial defect, as a corneal perforation can ensue. A limbal stem cell autograft would subject the fellow eye to unnecessary risk in the setting of poor visual potential. Penetrating keratoplasty is unlikely to provide a long-term solution and is also unnecessarily invasive.

pool.q: What refractive procedure would be preferred for restoring functional vision in a patient with keratoconus?
pool.rationale:
Intrastromal corneal ring segments have been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use in reducing or eliminating myopia and astigmatism in keratoconus patients who are no longer able to achieve adequate vision with their contact lenses or spectacles. The intent of intrastromal corneal ring segment placement is to restore functional vision and defer the need for corneal transplantation.
Corneal collagen crosslinking combines riboflavin, a naturally occurring photosensitizer, and ultraviolet A light to strengthen the biomechanical properties of the cornea. Although there may be a slight flattening of the cornea, the most important effect of this treatment is that it appears to stabilize the corneal curvature. The primary clinical application is as a treatment to prevent the progression of keratoconus and postrefractive ectasia.
Keratoconus is generally considered a contraindication to laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) and surface ablation; weakening of the cornea, as a result of the loss of structural integrity in LASIK flap creation and tissue removal, increases the risk of progressive ectasia. Although early case reports suggested that combining collagen crosslinking treatment with surface ablation or conductive keratoplasty may offer some benefit to keratoconus patients, the clinical evidence remains very preliminary.

pool.q: What stain would be best if Acanthamoeba keratitis is suspected?
pool.rationale: Acanthamoeba keratitis is a protozoal infection that can present in various ways, but is often associated with severe ocular pain, radial perineuritis, or a ring infiltrate. Preferred staining techniques for Acanthamoeba include: calcofluor white, giemsa, periodic acid-Schiff, and acridine orange stain. Other methods of detection include confocal microscopy or culture with nonnutrient agar with E coli or Enterobacter aerogenes. Crystal violet is used to stain amyloid. Gomori methenamine silver is used for fungi. Ziehl-Neelsen is used for acid-fast organisms.

pool.q: A number of cell types contribute to ocular immunological defense mechanisms. What cells function as dendritic antigen-presenting cells in the conjunctiva and cornea?
pool.rationale:
Langerhans cells are major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II+ dendritic antigen-presenting cells found in the conjunctiva and cornea. These cells uptake antigens and present them to CD4+ T cells, priming them to form an immune response. Corneal Langerhans cells are predominantly located in the limbus and corneal periphery.
Touton cells are multinucleated giant cells with foamy cytoplasm from high lipid content that can be seen in xanthogranulomas.

pool.q: What technique is the most useful in evaluating for lipid-deficient tear film?
pool.rationale:
A poor lipid layer can lead to tear film instability and increased tear evaporation. Measuring tear breakup time is a way to quantify tear film stability. To measure tear breakup time, the practitioner instills fluorescein in the patient's eyes and holds the eyelids open after a blink, counting the seconds until a dry spot appears. The appearance of a dry spot in less than 10 seconds is considered abnormal.
Schirmer testing uses filter paper to measure the amount of aqueous tear production over a period of time. Rose bengal and lissamine green stain epithelial cells of the cornea and conjunctiva when a disruption occurs in the protective mucin coating.

pool.q: What meibomian gland appearance is the final stage of severe chronic ocular rosacea?

options.b: atrophic glands without any expressible secretions
options.c: erythematous glands with thick white secretions

pool.rationale: The end stage of chronic ocular rosacea or severe meibomian gland dysfunction is involution and atrophy of the gland orifices and failure to produce expressible oil secretions. Transillumination or direct visualization of the palpebral conjunctiva may reveal shortened or absent vertical lines corresponding to the atrophied ducts. Increased thickness, turbidity, and inspissation of the meibomian gland secretions are all indicators of ongoing inflammation, but these represent earlier stages of the disease compared to gland atrophy.

pool.q: A 42-year-old man presents for a routine examination. On examination, the ophthalmologist notices a clear corneal depression and area of corneal thinning at the limbus, adjacent to a raised area of conjunctiva. There is no fluorescein uptake. What is the most appropriate treatment for this condition?

options.b: systemic immune suppression and topical lubrication
options.d: lid scrubs, warm compresses, and topical lubrication

pool.rationale:
A dellen is a small depression that occurs at the corneal limbus due to dehydration of the epithelium and stroma. Conjunctival elevation causes irregularity of the tear film, disrupting distribution from blinking in the involved area of cornea and leading to desiccation. Patching followed by topical lubrication can restore hydration of the stroma.
Systemic immune suppression along with topical lubrication can be considered for peripheral ulcerative keratitis. Although this may also result in thinning adjacent to the limbus, patients usually have an epithelial defect and corneal infiltrate. Additionally, the presence of raised conjunctiva may suggest dellen.
Lid scrubs, warm compresses, and topical lubrication can be used in the treatment of marginal keratitis, which is characterized by focal sterile infiltrates at the limbus from lid margin disease.

pool.q: What corneal condition has the highest chance of graft failure after penetrating keratoplasty in a pediatric patient?
pool.rationale:
In the case of corneal opacities from traumatic scars, infectious scars, and Peters anomaly type I, the pathology is generally limited to the cornea, with an otherwise normal anterior segment. This improves the prognosis for pediatric keratoplasty.
In the case of Peters anomaly type II, anterior segment findings can be more severe, including adhesions among cornea, iris, and lens. These associated anterior segment abnormalities lead to a higher chance of failure in pediatric keratoplasty.

pool.q: What appearance of the eyelid margin characterizes seborrheic blepharitis?

options.a: tarsal notching with missing lash follicles

pool.rationale: Seborrheic blepharitis describes the oily or flaky crusting that appears at the anterior eyelid margin. It may be associated with facial seborrhea or seborrhea in other areas of the body. Atrophic meibomian glands with telangiectasias are characteristic of ocular rosacea. Umbilicated pearly nodules may be seen in molluscum contagiosum. Tarsal notching with missing lash follicles may indicate the presence of a neoplasm or previous trauma.

pool.q: What gram-negative bacterium can penetrate an intact cornea epithelium?
pool.rationale:
Neisseria gonorrhoeae

The answer is Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Only a few organisms are able to invade an intact epithelium. They include Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Neisseria meningitides, Corynebacterium diphtheriae, Shigella species, Haemophilus aegyptius, and Listeria monocytogenes.
Staphylococcus aureus (gram-positive cocci) causes multiple ocular infections, including blepharitis, keratitis, and endophthalmitis, but it does not have the ability to penetrate an intact epithelium. Propionibacterium acnes (gram-positive rod) can become sequestered in the capsular bag following cataract surgery. It is associated with a delayed-onset chronic granulomatous uveitis with a white plaque on the posterior capsule. Treatment requires intravitreal antibiotics with possible vitrectomy to remove the capsular bag and intraocular lens. Streptococcus viridans (gram-positive cocci) is most commonly associated with crystalline keratopathy, in which the cornea has a branching, cracked-glass appearance. S viridans does not have the ability to penetrate an intact epithelium.

pool.q: A 57-year-old woman with a history of penetrating keratoplasty for a herpetic corneal scar presents with an endothelial rejection line, inferior graft edema, and a 2+ anterior chamber reaction. What is the most appropriate initial therapy?

options.b: frequent use of topical prednisolone with suppression dose of an oral antiviral agent
options.c: oral prednisone and a topical antiviral agent
options.d: frequent use of topical prednisolone alone

pool.rationale:
The presentation given is most consistent with corneal allograft rejection. The most appropriate therapy for new-onset endothelial rejection is hourly topical steroids, which may be combined with systemic steroids in severe cases. (Either dexamethasone 0.1% or prednisolone 1% eyedrops are used, as often as every 15 minutes to 2 hours, depending on the severity of the episode.) It is important to concurrently administer antiviral prophylaxis because of the known history of herpetic keratitis. As such, the most appropriate therapy is hourly topical prednisolone acetate 1% with oral acyclovir 400 mg BID. Topical prednisolone acetate 1% QID and oral acyclovir 400 mg 5 times daily is inadequate for suppressing the inflammation and endothelial cell damage caused by acute rejection. Topical steroids or oral acyclovir alone fail to address both problems in this scenario.
Bacterial, fungal, viral, or amebic keratitis can recur in a graft in the early postoperative period. In recurrent infections, medical treatment directed at the causative agents is the initial form of therapy.

pool.q: Factitious ocular surface disorders often present with what finding?

options.a: vital staining of conjunctiva in the medial and lateral interpalpebral space
options.b: vital staining in the inferior and nasal quadrants of the cornea
options.c: symblepharon formation with pooling of vital stain in the inferior fornix
options.d: vital staining of the superior bulbar conjunctiva

pool.rationale:
Factitious disorders include a spectrum of self-induced injuries with symptoms or physical findings that the patient intentionally produces. In factitious ocular surface disorder, there is usually evidence of mechanical injury to the inferior and nasal quadrants of the cornea and conjunctiva. The areas of involvement show sharply delineated borders. The conjunctival tissues usually show no evidence of inflammation of pathologic examination. Mucus-fishing syndrome and topical anesthetic abuse are common presentations of factitious ocular surface disorder.
Symblepharon would be more common in inflammatory states. While topical anesthetic abuse can produce a ring infiltrate, this is a sterile process and corneal scrapings and culture would produce no microbial etiology. Elastotic degeneration is seen with pterygium formation, which is common at the nasal and temporal aspects of the cornea and conjunctiva. Superior bulbar conjunctival staining would be seen in patients with superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis.

pool.q: What gonioscopic finding is important to look for in a patient with a history of blunt trauma?

options.c: blood vessels bridging across the angle

pool.rationale:
Wide ciliary body band, especially if sectoral or unilateral, is highly suggestive of angle recession. Other gonioscopic findings may include iris root tear or avulsion of the ciliary body. Patients with angle recession are at lifelong risk for developing glaucoma.
Neovascularization is not a common finding after blunt trauma. It is seen in ischemic disorders such as proliferative diabetic retinopathy and retinal vein occlusions.
Blood vessels bridging across the angle is a finding of Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis, and Sampaolesi line is seen in pigment dispersion and pseudoexfoliation syndrome.

pool.q: By what mechanism do oral antihistamines cause dry eye?
pool.rationale:
Many systemic medications, including antihistamines, antihypertensives such as propranolol and clonidine, decongestants such as pseudoephedrine, and antidepressants such as amitriptyline cause dry eye by decreasing aqueous tear production.
Increased (not decreased) tear film osmolarity can be associated with aqueous tear deficiency. Increased rate of tear evaporation, or evaporative dry eye, is caused by meibomian gland dysfunction. Decreased blink rate can be seen during some activities such as extensive reading or driving and in some neurologic conditions such as Parkinson disease.

pool.q: What property of adenovirus makes it resistant to routine disinfection precautions (eg, swabbing a tonometer tip with ethyl alcohol)?

options.b: presence of a double-stranded DNA genome
options.c: absence of glycoproteins in the capsid

pool.rationale: In contrast to herpes simplex virus (HSV), human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), and influenza virus, adenoviruses, and many other viruses responsible for infectious outbreaks, do not have a viral envelope. Viral envelopes are composed primarily of lipids and proteins, which render them more susceptible to heat, acids, and drying. Alcohol swabbing is sufficient to inactivate enveloped viruses. Adenoviruses, however, are surrounded only by a capsid of primarily glycoproteins, which are intrinsically more resistant to these same environmental stressors. For this reason, alcohol swabbing of a reusable tonometer tip is insufficient to prevent inoculation of subsequent patients in the setting of adenoviral exposure. Diluted bleach cleaning solution or disposable tonometer tips are necessary. Both HSV and adenovirus are characterized by a double-stranded DNA genome. Acanthamoeba, not adenovirus, can prolong survival by encysting itself in a dormant form.

pool.q: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment for mild to moderate scleritis?
pool.rationale: Scleritis is typically treated with oral agents. Several options are available: Mild-moderate scleritis can be treated with oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Severe scleritis or diseases not responsive to NSAIDs are treated with systemic corticosteroids (1 mg/kg/day with slow taper). In select cases, systemic immunosuppressive agents are needed, and should be used in consultation with an internist, oncologist, or rheumatologist.

pool.q: What systemic condition is associated with superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis?
pool.rationale: Superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis (SLK) is thought to result from mechanical trauma transmitted from the upper eyelid to the superior bulbar and tarsal conjunctiva. The condition is associated with autoimmune thyroid disease. It is typically seen in adult women (3:1 female to male), 20 to 70 years of age, with a median age of 50 years. It has also been associated with graft-vs-host disease and following blepharoplasty. Medical treatment is generally considered to be less effective than surgical treatment.

pool.q: What is the most common clinical manifestation of primary ocular herpes simplex?
pool.rationale: The most common presentation for primary ocular herpes is blepharoconjunctivitis. It is usually follicular in nature and accompanied by vesicles on the skin or eyelid margin that progress to blistered, crusted lesions. While epithelial keratitis can occur, stromal keratitis and uveitis are rare.

pool.q: What is thought to be the reason that pterygia occur more often on the nasal rather than the temporal side of the interpalpebral zone?

options.a: There is more Tenon tissue on the nasal side.
options.b: There are more stem cells residing in the nasal side.
options.c: The cornea is generally flatter on the temporal side.
options.d: The nose casts a shadow to the temporal interpalpebral zone.

pool.rationale: The predominance of pterygia on the nasal side in the interpalpebral zone is theorized to result from light passing medially through the cornea, focusing on the nasal limbal area, while the shadow of the nose reduces the intensity of light transmitted to the temporal limbus.

pool.q: If hypertonic saline solution (5% sodium chloride) fails to provide symptomatic relief from epithelial basement membrane dystrophy, what would be an appropriate next step?
pool.rationale: Corneal epithelial basement membrane dystrophy or map-dot-finger or Cogan microcystic dystrophy is characterized by an abnormality in epithelial turnover, maturation, and production of basement membrane. Initial therapy involves use of hypertonic (5%) saline, but this alone may be insufficient. Debriding the epithelium, or, if recalcitrant, stromal puncture or phototherapeutic keratectomy (PTK, not LASIK) could be considered. Acanthamoeba is an unlikely complication unless a chronic contact lens has been applied. A penetrating keratoplasty would be resurfaced by host epithelium, likely leading to recurrence.

pool.q: For a patient with conjunctival melanoma, what clinical feature increases the risk of regional lymph node metastasis?
pool.rationale: Conjunctival malignant melanoma that involves the palpebral conjunctiva is associated with an increased risk of lymphatic metastasis. Involvement of the limbus and bulbar conjunctiva is common and is not predictive of metastasis. Breslow score refers to the thickness of invasion of a cutaneous melanoma, and an increased Breslow score is associated with a higher chance of metastasis.

pool.q: What blood test should be ordered if on slit-lamp examination, the lens reveals reddish-brown pigment in the anterior capsule and subcapsular cortex in a stellate shape?
pool.rationale:
Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disease of copper metabolism. A "sunflower cataract" is sometimes seen as a result of cuprous oxide deposition in the anterior lens capsule and cortex. Another finding of Wilson disease is a Kayser-Fleischer ring, which is a golden brown coloration of the Descemet membrane. Cataracts may occur in any condition that causes hypocalcemia. The cataract is typically focal iridescent opacities within the cortex.
Other metabolic conditions known to cause cataract include diabetes mellitus, galactosemia, and myotonic dystrophy. Young patients with poorly controlled diabetic mellitus may develop an acute diabetic cataract or snowflake cataract consisting of bilateral, multiple gray-white subcapsular opacities. Vacuoles and clefts are also common in the lens of a person with diabetes. As diabetic patients age, they develop age-related changes similar to those in patients without diabetes, but the changes occur at a faster rate.
Galactosemia is an autosomal recessive disease that results in a lack of production of glucose from galactose. It is due to one of 3 enzyme deficiencies: galactose 1-phosphate uridyltransferase, galactokinase, or UDP galactose 4-epimerase. The most commonly involved enzyme is galactose 1-phosphate uridyltransferase. Patients develop an accumulation of galactose in the lens, which drives in water osmotically and causes an "oil droplet" cataract in the cortex on retroillumination. Other findings of this disease include hepatomegaly, malnutrition, jaundice, and intellectual deficiency.
Myotonic dystrophy is an autosomal dominant condition causing generalized muscle weakness, cardiac conduction defects, and frontal balding. Patients may develop iridescent opacities in the lens cortex with posterior subcapsular cataract.

pool.q: A 27-year-old woman presents with a complaint of eye irritation. She reports that she was using a tanning bed yesterday and removed her eye protection. On examination, she has eyelid edema, conjunctival hyperemia, and diffuse punctate keratitis of the right eye. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?

options.d: patching with cycloplegia and topical antibiotic ointment

pool.rationale: Ultraviolet (UV) radiation can be damaging to the corneal epithelium. Exposure to sunlamps and tanning beds can cause UV-induced injury. Treatment involves use of topical antibiotic ointment, cycloplegia, and patching to reduce discomfort from eyelid movement. Topical steroids or antihistamines are not indicated for this condition.

pool.q: A 70-year-old man presents with chronic unilateral crusting and discharge from the right lateral canthus. Gram stain of the discharge reveals numerous gram-negative cocci in pairs. What is the most likely pathogen?
pool.rationale:
Moraxella lacunata

The description is consistent with angular blepharitis, a relatively uncommon entity that may be mistaken for other forms of chronic lid margin inflammation. Angular blepharitis is classically caused by Moraxella lacunata (consistent with the Gram stain result of gram-negative cocci in pairs), although Staphylococcus aureus and herpes simplex virus are other possible etiologies. Chlamydia trachomatis is a potential cause of chronic follicular conjunctivitis, but it is not associated with angular blepharitis. Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Haemophilus influenzae can cause acute conjunctivitis, but they are not known to cause angular blepharitis.

pool.q: What would be an appropriate initial management of marginal corneal infiltrates associated with blepharoconjunctivitis?
pool.rationale:
Marginal corneal infiltrates associated with blepharoconjunctivitis are usually due to Staphylococcus aureus. Use of topical corticosteroids or a corticosteroid/antibiotic combination can be useful for treating acute inflammation. Management should also include therapy for blepharitis with warm compresses, lid scrubs, antibiotic ointment to lid margins, or topical antibiotics. Also, oral tetracyclines or erythromycin can be considered.
Topical cyclosporine would not be a good option, as it is not an ideal agent to treat acute inflammation. Surgery or laser procedures should be avoided in patients with an acute inflammation. Artificial tears would not be useful for treatment of the inflammation.

pool.q: What clinical finding makes the diagnosis of mucous membrane pemphigoid more likely than pseudopemphigoid?
pool.rationale:
Mucous membrane pemphigoid (MMP) is a chronic cicatrizing conjunctivitis of autoimmune reaction etiology. It primarily involves the conjunctiva; however, it frequently affects other mucous membranes including the mouth and oropharynx, genitalia, and anus.
Pseudopemphigoid has been associated with long-term use of certain topical medications. Case reports have implicated pilocarpine, epinephrine, timolol, idoxuridine, echothiophate iodide, and demecarium bromide.
Pemphigoid and pseudopemphigoid share several features, including conjunctival hyperemia, papillary conjunctivitis, conjunctival erosions, conjunctival subepithelial fibrosis, symblepharon, tear deficiency, and abnormal position of the eyelids and eyelashes, including entropion, trichiasis, and distichiasis. However, it would not be typical for pseudopemphigoid to have other (nonocular) findings, such as skin lesions and/or oral or respiratory lesions.

pool.q: What systemic antibiotic can be given as a single dose to treat adult chlamydial conjunctivitis?
pool.rationale:
Azithromycin 1g PO administered once is an acceptable treatment for adult chlamydial conjunctivitis (it may be necessary in some cases to retreat at 1 week). For this reason, it may be a preferable choice for patients with a history of poor compliance. The other 3 antibiotic choices are also effective therapies, but they must be administered over a 7-day period. Sexual partners should be treated concurrently to prevent reinfection.
Currently, 1 of the following oral antibiotic regimens is recommended:
  • azithromycin 1000 mg  PO single dose
  • doxycycline 100 mg PO BID x 7days
  • tetracycline 250 mg PO QID x 7 days
  • erythromycin 500 mg PO QID x 7 days

pool.q: A 20-year-old, otherwise healthy patient presents with severe pain, photophobia, and blurry vision 5 days after bilateral photorefractive keratectomy (PRK). Examination reveals an 8 mm epithelial defect with a faint ring infiltrate and small hypopyon in both eyes. Gram stain and potassium hydroxide (KOH) prep are negative for organisms. Cultures are negative and there is minimal improvement on topical fortified antibiotics over the next several days. What is the most important history to obtain?

options.a: history of showering with contact lenses
options.b: use of any nonprescribed eye drops
options.d: history of cold sores or fever blisters

pool.rationale:
This history is concerning for anesthetic abuse. Patients may be reluctant to reveal this information, but it is critical to ask the patient directly and nonjudgmentally in suspected cases. The most suspicious elements are the patient's young age, the bilateral involvement of the eyes, and the description of a non-healing defect with an early ring infiltrate.
Although herpetic disease could present with a non-healing ulcer after a surface procedure, it would be unlikely to present bilaterally. A history of showering with contact lenses is important when considering Acanthamoeba, but in this case the rapid onset makes a toxic etiology more likely. Use of oral pain medications is an important part of the medical history, but it does not help to narrow the differential diagnosis.

pool.q: Neurotrophic keratopathy is most frequently encountered as a long-term consequence of what type of infectious keratitis?
pool.rationale:
Viral keratitis, specifically herpes simplex and herpes zoster keratitis, is most commonly associated with long-term corneal hypoesthesia and neurotrophic keratopathy. Although some degree of corneal hypoesthesia can occur after other forms of infectious keratitis, viral keratitis is by far the most common. pool.q: What is the most appropriate initial management of a patient with an acute corneal injury involving tree sap?
pool.rationale:
Ocular contact with tree sap (particularly those from the pencil tree and manchineel tree) may result in keratoconjunctivitis, epithelial defects, stromal infiltration, and opportunistic infection. The most important initial management is copious irrigation, similar to management of a chemical injury.
To minimize the risk of potentiating a fungal infection, topical corticosteroids are not recommended in the acute setting. Empiric fungal therapy, however, is not routinely recommended unless evidence of infectious keratitis develops, and at that point culture and/or biopsy should be performed to determine the infectious agent. Occlusive patching is not routinely recommended in the setting of vegetative trauma.

pool.q: What topical treatment regimen is recommended for ocular surface squamous neoplasia?

options.a: topical mitomycin C (MMC) 1% 4 times daily for 3–4 months
options.b: topical prednisolone acetate 1% 4 times/day for 3-4 months
options.c: topical interferon-a2b 1 million IU/mL 4 times daily for 3–4 months

pool.rationale:
2b 1 million IU/mL 4 times daily for 3–4 months

Several topical therapies can be used to treat ocular surface squamous neoplasia. Topical interferon-α2b (IFN-α2b) 1 million IU/mL is typically given 4 times daily until clinical resolution occurs, usually within 2 to 4 months. Several additional months of treatment might be beneficial; recent evidence indicates that residual tumor might be present for up to 3 months following clinical resolution. Subconjunctival/perilesional IFN-α2b (3 million IU in 0.5 mL) can be given weekly in addition to, or as an alternative to, topical drops, especially if patient adherence is an issue. Subconjunctival IFN-α2b is associated with flulike symptoms in 10% of patients.
Mitomycin C (MMC) can be used for a shorter duration — typically weeks rather than months — but might have greater adverse effects, including surface toxicity and potential stem cell deficiency. Topical MMC 0.02% or 0.04% is typically administered 4 times daily for 1 week, followed by a 1-week structured treatment interruption (drug holiday), for a maximum of 3 or 4 treatment cycles.
Topical 5-fluorouracil 1% can be given 4 times daily for 1 month, with at least several months off if repeated; alternatively, it can be given 4 times daily for 1 week, followed by a 3-week structured treatment interruption, until resolution, for a maximum of 3 cycles.
Application of topical corticosteroids may help with the surface toxicity. Placement of punctal plugs reduces the likelihood of systemic absorption and helps prevent punctal stenosis.

pool.q: A 54-year-old man on amiodarone for cardiac arrhythmia is found to have yellow-white deposits in a whorl-like pattern in the inferocentral corneal epithelium of both eyes. What is the most appropriate management of the corneal deposits?
pool.rationale: Cornea verticillata, or vortex keratopathy, manifests as a whorl-like pattern of golden brown or gray deposits in the inferior interpalpebral aspect of the cornea. Some systemic medications can bind with the cellular lipids of the basal epithelial layer of the cornea to cause this appearance. The anti-arrhythmic medication amiodarone is the most common cause of corneal verticillata. It is unusual for these deposits to result in reduction of vision or ocular symptoms; therefore, treatments such as superficial keratectomy with excimer laser are not necessary. It is acceptable for the patient to continue on the recommended dose of systemic medication.

pool.q: One week after undergoing epithelial debridement for chronic recurrent corneal erosions, a patient returns with persistent pain. The examination reveals a 7 mm nonhealing epithelial defect without any visible corneal infiltrate or anterior chamber reaction. The patient's current medications are topical ofloxacin 0.3% QID and topical ketorolac 0.5% QID. What is the most appropriate management?

options.b: start Muro 128 (5% sodium chloride) eye drops
options.c: perform anterior stromal micropuncture in the area of the epithelial defect

pool.rationale:
The most important first step in this scenario is to discontinue the topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drop (ketorolac), which may delay epithelialization in some patients. Topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) can even cause corneal melts or even corneal perforations.
Topical ofloxacin is unlikely to be the cause of the persistent epithelial defect and should not be discontinued without starting an alternative prophylactic antibiotic.
Anterior stromal micropuncture may be an effective treatment for recurrent erosions but is better performed through loose, intact epithelium than to the bed of an abrasion.
Muro 128 drops are another treatment for preventing recurrent erosions, but they have limited benefit in the setting of a nonhealing epithelial defect.

pool.q: What is the best way to manage uveal prolapse when it occurs during an acute open-globe repair?
pool.rationale:
If uvea or retina (seen as translucent, tan tissue with extremely fine vessels) protrudes, the surgeon can reposit it, using a gentle sweeping technique through a separate limbal incision, with the assistance of viscoelastic injection to keep the anterior chamber formed. Only in cases of frankly necrotic, macerated, or contaminated tissue should prolapsed uveal tissue be excised.
Cauterization of uveal tissue would not be appropriate. Reconstruction of iris tissue, using techniques such as the McCannel suture, may be indicated in a follow-up surgery, but not during the repair of an acute open globe.

pool.q: What is the appropriate microscope cell staining technique to confirm the diagnosis of adult chlamydial conjunctivitis?
pool.rationale:
Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular bacterium that is best visualized with Giemsa staining. The characteristic appearance is intracytoplasmic basophilic inclusion bodies within epithelial cells.
Acid-fast staining aids in the identification of Mycobacteria species.
Calcofluor white stain is useful for visualizing fungal elements.
Gram staining is appropriate for typical bacterial infections but does not readily identify atypical bacteria, including Chlamydia species.

pool.q: The refractive correction of the intrastromal corneal ring devices (INTACS) procedure is titrated by choosing what factor of the implant?
pool.rationale:
The amount of correction achieved is related to the thickness of the ring segments, not to their diameter (they have a fixed outer diameter), nor their material (they are all made of polymethylmethacrylate [PMMA]), and not to their implantation depth.
When performing INTACS, increasing the ring thickness will achieve a reduced corneal arc length (flattening effect) and thus greater correction of myopia. An advantage of INTACS is that the effect of myopia correction can be titrated. For example, if a patient remains undercorrected with a 0.325 mm ring, it can be exchanged for a thicker ring (eg, 0.350 mm or 0.400 mm); if a patient is overcorrected, a thinner ring can be exchanged to reduce the amount of myopia correction. The depth of the ring segments must always be between 68% and 70% for this procedure and is not varied.

pool.q: A 67-year-old man visits the ophthalmologist for an examination. He has a history of hypercalcemia, renal failure, and a recent work-up including serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP), which demonstrated a monoclonal spike. What ocular finding is associated with his underlying condition?
pool.rationale:
Hypercalcemia, renal failure, and monoclonal spike on SPEP are associated with multiple myeloma. Ocular findings associated with multiple myeloma include crystalline deposits in all layers of the cornea (or in the conjunctiva), hyperviscosity of retinal vasculature, pars plana cysts, or proptosis from orbital bony invasion.
Sea-fan retinal neovascularization is a characteristic of sickle cell retinopathy. Blue sclera is characteristic of osteogenesis imperfecta, a condition caused by a mutation in type I collagen. Corneal verticillata are seen in Fabry disease, an X-linked recessive condition characterized by deficiency of α-galactosidase A. Verticillata can also be caused by multiple medications, such as amiodarone or phenothiazines or netarsudil.

pool.q: In order to be considered acute graft-versus-host disease, within what time period following bone marrow transplantation do symptoms need to present?
pool.rationale: Graft-versus-host disease is a complication that can occur following allogeneic bone marrow transplantation, wherein the grafted cells attack the host tissue. Ocular surface manifestations can include conjunctival inflammation and severe keratoconjunctivitis sicca. Acute graft-versus-host disease occurs within 3 months of transplantation, although most ocular manifestations are seen in chronic graft-versus host-disease (greater than 3 months from transplantation).

pool.q: For what type of corneal scarring is phototherapeutic keratectomy (PTK) contraindicated?

options.a: anterior stromal scarring from previous bacterial keratitis
options.b: deep central scarring from herpes simplex keratitis
options.c: subepithelial scarring from anterior basement membrane dystrophy (ABMD)

pool.rationale: Phototherapeutic keratectomy (PTK) is indicated for the treatment of visually significant anterior (limited to the superficial one-third) stromal opacity or irregular astigmatism due to anterior scarring. Deeper scars are not amenable to PTK, due to the necessity of tissue destruction and the resulting corneal destabilization and severe hyperopic shift. Previous herpetic keratitis is also a relative contraindication to excimer laser smoothing. Anterior scars caused by previous bacterial keratitis, central islands following refractive surgery, and subepithelial scarring secondary to ABMD are all acceptable candidates for PTK.

pool.q: What is the most common etiology of isolated episcleritis?
pool.rationale: The majority of cases of isolated episcleritis are idiopathic. Autoimmune conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and Wegener granulomatosis have all been associated with episcleritis, but a serologic workup is rarely indicated in the absence of other systemic findings.

pool.q: What is the most appropriate initial treatment for Candida keratitis?
pool.rationale: Topical amphotericin B, and more recently voriconazole, has been advocated for treating keratitis caused by yeasts such as Candida. Topical amphotericin B is also recommended for Aspergillus keratitis. Natamycin 5% is more effective against filamentous fungi such as Fusarium species and is thus first-line treatment for most fungal keratitis in the southern United States. Because of its systemic toxicity and irregular penetration to the cornea, intravenous amphotericin B should be avoided for keratitis.

pool.q: What organism causes ocular toxocariasis?
pool.rationale:
Toxocara canis

Ocular toxocariasis (also termed ocular larval migrans) is a rare condition resulting from tissue invasion by the second-stage larvae of Toxocara canis or cati. Ocular larval migrans, with sparing of the viscera, often occurs in older children. In contrast, visceral larval migrans typically occurs in younger children.
Toxoplasma gondii causes toxoplasmosis, which is a much more common retinochoroiditis and may be acquired or congenital.
The Brucella species may cause a systemic infection in humans after exposure to infected animals, typically via ingestion of unpasteurized milk or cheese products.
Onchocerciasis, caused by the filarial parasite Onchocerca volvulus, is one of the leading causes of blindness in sub-Saharan Africa. The flies that carry the parasite breed in fast-flowing streams, giving the disease its common name, "river blindness."

pool.q: What is the appropriate surgical therapy for visually significant Salzmann nodular degeneration?
pool.rationale:
Salzmann nodular degeneration refers to grayish subepithelial nodules that typically occur following previous inflammatory or mechanical insult to the cornea. They can also be idiopathic. These changes are typically confined to the very superficial anterior stroma and are amenable to debridement with superficial keratectomy.
LASIK would not be a good option, as flap creation would preserve the pathologic changes. Deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty is unnecessarily invasive for a superficial condition. Limbal stem cell resection is reserved for the treatment of focal limbal stem cell deficiency causing visual impairment. This treatment would not be indicated for Salzmann nodular degeneration.

pool.q: For a patient with an intraocular pressure (IOP) of 18 mm Hg measured by applanation tonometry and a central corneal thickness of 490 μm, what is the most likely IOP upon entering the anterior chamber (ie, the manometric IOP)?

options.d: cannot be predicted with this information

pool.rationale:
Applanation tonometry assumes certain properties of the cornea when IOP is calculated. Measurement with the Goldmann tonometer is most accurate when the central corneal thickness (CCT) is 520 μm. Thicker corneas resist the deformation inherent in most methods of tonometry, resulting in an overestimation of IOP, while thinner corneas may give an artificially low reading. Although the exact conversion factor is not universally agreed upon (typically around 1 mm Hg of deviation for every 10 to 15 μm deviation from normal corneal thickness), the pattern has been well established.
The most likely IOP upon entering the anterior chamber can be predicted with the information provided in the stem about CCT and intraocular pressure measured by applanation. The given CCT is less than 520 μm, and thus will give a falsely low reading on applanation. The most likely IOP upon entering the anterior chamber would be less than 18 mm Hg if the CCT were thicker or greater than 520 μm and applanation measured a higher-than-true IOP.

pool.q: For a patient with acute Stevens-Johnson syndrome and conjunctival involvement, what surgical treatment is the most beneficial?
pool.rationale: Amniotic membrane grafting has been established as an effective therapy for patients with conjunctival inflammation secondary to Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS). Conjunctival resection is indicated in some cases of severe peripheral ulcerative keratitis or Mooren ulcer, but it plays no role in the management of SJS. Punctal cauterization can be employed as a long-term strategy for severe dry eye resulting from SJS, but it would not be indicated in the acute setting. A Gunderson flap can be employed for select nonhealing corneal ulcers, but it would not be a good choice in the setting of SJS.

pool.q: When performing cataract surgery in patients with endothelial dystrophy, what step should be taken to reduce operative risks?

options.a: performing phacoemulsification in the anterior chamber to avoid posterior capsule rupture
options.b: use of a hyperosmotic balanced salt solution (BSS)
options.c: frequent use of a dispersive viscoelastic
options.d: use of capsule dye to ensure safety during capsulorrhexis

pool.rationale: Endothelial dystrophy (or Fuchs endothelial dystrophy) ranges from asymptomatic to a decompensated corneal edema.  The condition shows variable autosomal dominant transmission and can be sporadic.  Endothelial cell counts of less than 1000/mm2 or the presence of epithelial edema suggests caution and the possibility that the cornea might decompensate with surgery.  Techniques during cataract surgery would be aimed at reducing the amount of ultrasound power used and optimizing the distance of the ultrasound from the corneal endothelium.  Using the pulse-and-burst mode of phacoemulsification reduces overall ultrasound power used.  Frequent use of viscoelastic will help protect the endothelium. Using hyperosmotic topical drops is sometimes used to aid in corneal edema, but not hyperosmotic BSS during surgery.  Using a capsule dye is a technique used for dense cataracts, not a technique for endothelial dystrophy.

pool.q: For the initial management of early and peripheral contact lens-related microbial keratitis, what topical antibiotic is most appropriate as monotherapy?
pool.rationale: Initial treatment of a contact lens-related microbial keratitis should include a broad-spectrum activity against gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria. Fluoroquinolones, particularly fourth-generation fluoroquinolones, have good coverage against most gram-positive and gram-negative organisms implicated in contact lens-related microbial keratitis. Sulfonamides, penicillins, and first-generation cephalosporins lack adequate coverage against gram-negative organisms, most notably Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

pool.q: What condition is phlyctenulosis usually associated with?
pool.rationale: Phlyctenules are a delayed or cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction to staphylococcus or other microbial antigens, not meibomian gland dysfunction, seborrheic blepharitis, or vernal conjunctivitis. They are characterized by focal gray or yellow elevations in cornea, limbal region, or conjunctiva.

pool.q: In herpes zoster ophthalmicus, what is the most typical location of vesicular lesions?
pool.rationale: The presence of vesicular involvement of the upper eyelid (CN V1) is 1 feature that can distinguish herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO) from other dermatomal involvement. One would expect to see involvement of the forehead and upper lid as part of V1 zoster dermatitis, but the lower eyelid is supplied by V2 and is not as commonly associated with HZO. The cheek and scalp are also not generally involved in HZO. In immunosuppressed patients, more than 1 branch of CN V may be affected simultaneously.

pool.q: When an inheritance pattern is present in Fuchs endothelial dystrophy, what type of pattern is most common?
pool.rationale:
Fuchs endothelial dystrophy is characterized by corneal guttae and decreased endothelial cell function, which lead to decreased vision. Cases without known inheritance are common, but when an inheritance pattern is present, it is usually autosomal dominant.
To manifest an autosomal recessive dystrophy, an individual must receive a genetic mutation from both parents who, although carriers of the mutation, are usually unaffected. Macular corneal dystrophy is an example of autosomal recessive inheritance.
X-linked dominant inheritance occurs when a genetic mutation is carried on the X chromosome and manifests in both male and female carriers. Incontinentia pigmenti is an example of X-linked dominant inheritance.
Mitochondrial inheritance occurs when a genetic mutation found on mitochondrial DNA is passed from mother to offspring. Leber hereditary optic neuropathy is an example of mitochondrial inheritance.

pool.q: What is the most effective immediate treatment for a symptomatic corneal infiltrate caused by staphylococcal marginal keratitis?
pool.rationale: The limbus plays an important role in immune-mediated corneal disorders. The limbus has a population of antigen-presenting cells (APCs) that constitutively express MHC class II antigens and are capable of efficient mobilization and induction of T-cell responses. Therefore, immune-related corneal changes often occur in a peripheral location adjacent to the limbus. In addition, because the peripheral cornea is adjacent to the vascularized (posterior) limbus, circulating immune cells, immune complexes, and complement factors tend to deposit adjacent to the terminal capillary loops of the limbal vascular arcades, thereby producing a variety of immune phenomena that manifest in the corneal periphery.

pool.q: What test is most appropriate to confirm the presence of corneal guttae?
pool.rationale:
Imaging of the corneal endothelium can be accomplished by specular microscopy or confocal microscopy. Typically, a slit-lamp examination is sufficient to diagnose corneal guttae, but either of these tests may be useful in equivocal cases.
Pachymetry may be elevated in patients with corneal guttae, but it does not confirm the diagnosis. Ultrasound biomicroscopy is better suited for imaging larger structures of the angle or the ciliary body and cannot identify corneal guttae. Anterior segment OCT can provide corneal thickness and curvature measurements, but it is not suitable for identifying corneal guttae.

pool.q: What culture media is best suited for identifying mycobacterial infections?
pool.rationale:
Mycobacterium can be cultured on Löwenstein-Jensen medium for identification as the causative agent of a corneal infection. Thioglycollate broth is useful for culturing aerobic and anaerobic bacteria. Chocolate agar is most effective for identifying aerobic bacteria. Buffered charcoal-yeast extract agar can be used to identify Acanthamoeba infections.

pool.q: What vital dye is most likely to produce symptoms of ocular irritation?
pool.rationale: Ocular surface damage is commonly assessed by staining with fluorescein, rose bengal, and/or lissamine green. Of these, rose bengal staining is the most poorly tolerated and frequently causes some irritation and reflex tearing. Rose bengal stains the conjunctivae to a greater extent than the cornea and signifies areas of devitalized epithelial cells. Trypan blue is used in vivo for staining of anterior capsule during cataract surgery, assessing trabeculectomy bleb function, and staining of trabecular meshwork during angle-based minimally invasive glaucoma surgery (MIGS) procedures. Fluorescein sodium dye is most commonly clinically used and is relatively well tolerated. Fluorescein stains the cornea to a greater extent than the conjunctiva and signifies areas where the epithelial cells have desquamated. Lissamine green is usually well tolerated.

pool.q: What is the best noninvasive way to visualize the cysts pathognomonic of Acanthamoeba keratitis?
pool.rationale:
Confocal microscopy has demonstrated efficacy in the early diagnosis of patients with Acanthamoeba. It allows rapid identification of acanthamoebal cysts with a relatively high sensitivity and specificity, although it requires a skilled observer to interpret the images.
Sclerotic scatter is useful for demonstrating subtle pathology but is inadequate to resolve microscopic cysts. Specular microscopy allows imaging of the corneal endothelium, but is not considered useful in the diagnosis of Acanthamoeba keratitis. Optical coherence tomography can provide cross-sectional information about corneal pathology but is inadequate to resolve microscopic structures the size of Acanthamoeba cysts.

pool.q: What rheumatologic condition is most frequently associated with peripheral ulcerative keratitis?

options.b: granulomatosis with polyangiitis (also termed Wegener granulomatosis)

pool.rationale: Rheumatoid arthritis is the condition most frequently associated with peripheral ulcerative keratitis, and testing for rheumatoid factor (RF) is warranted as part of the systemic evaluation. Systemic lupus erythematosus, granulomatosis with polyangiitis (also termed Wegener granulomatosis), and ulcerative colitis are also associated with peripheral ulcerative keratitis, but they are less commonly present.

pool.q: An asymptomatic patient presents for a routine examination. The ophthalmologist discovers longstanding traumatic mydriasis. What is the appropriate next step?

options.b: Begin a trial of topical corticosteroids.
options.d: Begin a trial of pilocarpine drops.

pool.rationale: Given that the patient is asymptomatic, observation is the best choice. If the patient were to develop symptoms, a trial of medical therapy would involve less risk than surgery.

pool.q: What is a contraindication for using corneal tissue for transplantation?
pool.rationale:
The Eye Bank Association of America has a list of exclusion criteria regarding donation of tissue for corneal transplantation. Leukemia, active disseminated lymphoma, and malignant tumors of the anterior segment or known adenocarcinoma in the eye of primary or metastatic origin are contraindications for donation. Lung adenocarcinoma that has not metastasized to the eye is not on the list of exclusion criteria. A history of sarcoidosis without active ocular or intraocular inflammation would not be a contraindication. Psychiatric disorders are not part of the criteria contraindicating donor cornea use.
Criteria for exclusion include:
  • Death of unknown cause
  • Congenital rubella
  • Reye syndrome within the past 3 months
  • Neurodegenerative conditions including prion disease (eg, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy)
  • Infectious conditions including human immunodeficiency virus, hepatitis, and active bacterial/viral encephalitis or bacterial/fungal endocarditis, suspected rabies or history of being bitten within the past 6 months
  • Down syndrome (exclusion criterion for penetrating and anterior lamellar keratoplasties)
  • Intrinsic eye disease including retinoblastoma, malignant tumors of the anterior segment, or known adenocarcinoma in the eye of primary or metastatic origin, active ocular or intraocular inflammation, congenital or acquired disorders of the eye that would preclude a successful outcome
  • Leukemias
  • Active disseminated lymphomas
  • Behavioral criteria: High-risk behavior (eg, intravenous drug use or incarceration in prison)
  • Prior refractive corneal surgery with the exception that previous laser refractive surgery may not disqualify for use in endothelial keratoplasty
  • Positive test for anti-HIV-1/anti-HIV-2, nonreactive for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and anti-HCV antibody

(A figure accompanies this rationale on the section page.)

pool.q: What is the optimal illumination method to view the corneal endothelium by slit-lamp examination?
pool.rationale: Specular reflection is best for viewing the corneal endothelium with the slit lamp. The other 3 methods listed are used to view other parts of the cornea: Sclerotic scatter is used for edema, retroillumination is used for posterior capsule and corneal opacities, and proximal illumination is used for lesions and corneal foreign bodies.

pool.q: The diagnosis of seasonal allergic conjunctivitis can be confirmed by finding a predominance of what cell types in a conjunctival scraping?
pool.rationale: All 3 specific types of ocular allergy: seasonal allergic conjunctivitis, vernal conjunctivitis, and atopic keratoconjunctivitis, have some element of type 1 hypersensitivity reaction caused by the interaction between an allergen and specific immunoglobulin E (IgE) antibodies on the surface of mast cells in the conjunctiva. In seasonal allergic conjunctivitis, conjunctival scrapings reveal eosinophils, a finding that is almost diagnostic of an allergic response.

pool.q: A 56-year-old man with decreased vision has a markedly enlarged corneal diameter and visually significant cataract; the dilated exams are normal for both eyes. Preoperative measurements for cataract surgery show normal axial length with white-to-white measurements of 14.5 mm in both eyes. During cataract surgery, what complication is the patient at increased risk for?
pool.rationale:
Megalocornea is a condition with bilateral, nonprogressive corneal enlargement that usually shows X-linked inheritance. In this condition, the cornea is histologically normal, but its diameter is greater than 13 mm. Megalocornea is associated with zonular instability, so there are additional risks for these eyes during cataract surgery. Megalocornea is not associated with an increased risk of bleeding or malignant glaucoma. Nanophthalmic eyes are associated with an increased risk of choroidal effusion during cataract surgery.
Lens instability and subluxation, iridodonesis, and poor zonular integrity are also associated with megalocornea and present additional risks and challenges in the management of cataracts, particularly in terms of the selection and placement of an intraocular lens (IOL) after cataract surgery. If the lens is of normal size, an IOL can be inserted in the capsular bag. A capsular tension ring may be placed to reduce stress on the zonular fibers. Standard-sized posterior chamber lenses are typically too short to be fixated in the ciliary sulcus, and anterior chamber lenses are similarly problematic in the enlarged anterior chamber. If zonular support is insufficient or capsular volume too great to allow stable IOL centration, an iris clip or iris-sutured lens may be the best option.

pool.q: A 43-year-old woman presents with an iris elevation and corresponding pigmented mass visible on gonioscopy. What is the best imaging modality to further investigate this lesion?
pool.rationale:
High-frequency ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM) provides high-resolution in vivo imaging of the anterior segment. Tissues visualized include the cornea, anterior and posterior iris, ciliary body, zonules, angle structures, and anterior lens capsule. UBM allows a view through an opaque cornea and total hyphema. UBM is helpful in the assessment of ciliary body pathology, including cysts and tumors. Its major advantage is in visualizing structures behind the iris.
B-scan ultrasonography is more useful in detailing posterior segment pathology. A CT scan images structures external to the globe, and is used in assessing, for example, orbital and facial pathology. Anterior segment OCT provides high-resolution imaging of the anterior segment but is best used for structures anterior to the iris plane.
