pool.q: For 2 weeks, a patient with past ocular herpes simplex keratitis has had ocular redness and irritation. What slit-lamp finding is most strongly suggestive of an active epithelial herpes simplex infection?

options.a: terminal bulbs on linear epithelial lesions

pool.rationale:
Herpes simplex virus (HSV) epithelial keratitis typically presents as a linear lesion with dichotomous branching and terminal bulbs at the ends of branches. Ciliary flush and conjunctival injection usually coincide with the corneal findings. With worsening, the terminal bulbs can coalesce into a geographic ulcer.
The other presentations are not typical for HSV epithelial keratitis. Mucous epithelial plaques and filaments with punctate staining are consistent with dryness, while a hypopyon suggests severe intraocular inflammation, often seen with infection

pool.q: What finding would support the decision for pterygium excision?

options.a: pterygium excision of the contralateral eye
options.d: deposition of iron at the leading edge

pool.rationale:
The most widely accepted indications for pterygium excision include induced astigmatism and chronic symptomatic irritation. Induced astigmatism is most commonly with-the-rule, with relative flattening occurring in the axis of the pterygium.
A history of pterygium excision in the contralateral eye may indicate a propensity for progression but is not, in and of itself, an indication for surgery.
Deposition of iron at the leading edge (Stocker line) is indicative of relative stability and is not an indication for excision.
Increased thickness on pachymetry may be observed, owing to the pterygium's added thickness on the underlying cornea.

pool.q: How can the technique of specular reflection with a slit lamp be optimized to evaluate endothelial cell morphology?

options.a: Set the slit-beam arm at an angle of 60° from the viewing arm and use a short slit.
options.b: Direct a narrow slit beam at the nasal or temporal limbus.
options.c: Use a wide diffuse slit-lamp beam.

pool.rationale:
Specular reflection is mainly used to examine the corneal endothelium (second Purkinje light reflex), although it can also examine corneal epithelium and lens epithelium. Endothelial cell morphology is typically viewed under high magnification using only 1 ocular.
The examiner can enhance this specular reflection by placing a light beam at an appropriate angle, revealing the corneal endothelium. Following are the steps for examining the corneal endothelium with specular reflection:
  • Begin by setting the slit-beam arm at an angle of 60° from the viewing arm and using a short slit or 0.2-mm spot.
  • Identify the very bright mirror image of the lightbulb’s filament and the paired epithelial and endothelial Purkinje light reflexes.
  • Superimpose the corneal endothelial light reflex onto the filament’s mirror image, giving a bright glare.
  • Use the joystick to move the biomicroscope slightly forward in order to focus the endothelial reflex.
A wide diffuse beam is used to optimize diffuse illumination. A tall wide beam directed onto the limbal area is used to optimize sclerotic scatter.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: The ends of herpes zoster dendritiform lesions are typically what shape?
pool.rationale: The dendritic epithelial keratitis common in ophthalmic zoster is actually caused by herpes zoster pseudodendrites. These pseudodendrites, as distinguished from true dendrites in herpes simplex virus epithelial keratitis, have blunt ends rather than terminal bulbs, have little epithelial ulceration, and stain poorly with fluorescein and rose bengal. Additionally, pseudodendrites typically have a more raised, plaque-like appearance.

pool.q: Combined hearing loss and corneal findings are seen in what clinical entity?
pool.rationale: Stromal interstitial keratitis can be associated with a variety of systemic diseases including autoimmune (systemic lupus erythematosus, polyarteritis nodosa), protozoan (trypanosomiasis [sleeping sickness]), plasmodium [malaria], leishmaniasis), worms (onchocerciasis [river blindness], schistosomiasis [bilharzia], taenia solium [cysticercosis]), viral (herpes zoster, rubeola, vaccinia, herpes simplex virus, mumps, influenza, Epstein-Barr virus), bacterial (Treponema pallidum, Mycobacterium spp, Borrelia spp, Leptospira spp), and in conditions with unknown underlying etiology, such as Cogan interstitial keratitis. The latter clinical entity is associated with interstitial keratitis, vertigo, and hearing loss. Early diagnosis of Cogan syndrome is vital because the syndrome can include systemic vasculitis as one of its findings, which can lead to death if not adequately treated.

pool.q: What best describes the origin of conjunctival melanoma?

options.a: It always arises from a preexisting conjunctival nevus.
options.b: It always arises from conjunctival melanocytes.
options.d: It always arises from primary acquired melanosis.

pool.rationale: Conjunctival melanomas may arise from PAM (70%) or nevi (5%) or may arise de novo (25%). A PAM lesion should be removed if it involves greater than 2 clock-hours, or has progressive enlargement, a nodular component, feeder vessels, or thickening. It should then be biopsied to identify whether atypia is present and whether it has converted to melanoma.

pool.q: A 75-year-old patient presents for evaluation of blunt trauma to the right eye from a fall sustained one day previously. Vision is 20/50 in the affected eye. The slit-lamp examination is remarkable for a formed anterior chamber with a teardrop-shaped pupil. Two clock hours of iris are prolapsed through the previous temporal clear corneal phacoemulsification incision. The extruded iris tissue appears viable but is noted to have a thin translucent membrane adherent to the stromal surface. In addition to surgical repair of the laceration, what is the most appropriate management?

options.a: Reposit the prolapsed iris tissue, with removal of the membrane.
options.b: Reposit the prolapsed iris tissue after swabbing the membrane for cultures.
options.c: Excise the prolapsed iris tissue and the membrane en-bloc.
options.d: Reposit the prolapsed iris tissue, without removal of the membrane.

pool.rationale: Whenever possible, viable uveal tissue should be reposited during surgical repair of a ruptured globe. In this case, the description is consistent with iris prolapse and early epithelialization of the iris surface from the cornea or conjunctival epithelium. As the iris tissue is noted to be viable and the injury is recent, the most appropriate option is to peel off any adherent membranes and reposit the iris tissue. Repositing the tissue without peeling off the membranes would increase the risk of developing epithelial ingrowth. Similarly, culturing the membrane without excising it would also be inappropriate. Excision of the prolapsed iris tissue should only be performed when the iris tissue is visibly necrotic or macerated beyond repair.

pool.q: What organism commonly causes angular blepharoconjunctivitis?
pool.rationale:
Moraxella lacunata

Moraxella lacunata is a common cause of angular blepharoconjunctivitis. Propionibacterium acnes is a slow-growing organism that can be seen in pseudophakic chronic endophthalmitis. Streptococcus pneumoniae and Chlamydia trachomatis are both causes of bacterial conjunctivitis.

pool.q: In a patient with fungal keratitis, what finding confers the most guarded (ominous) prognosis?
pool.rationale: Invasion of fungus into the sclera is a potentially globe-threatening complication. Scleral extension can precede intraocular infection and is particularly concerning because infected tissue may no longer be cleared by surgical grafting. Extension into the sclera or anterior chamber lowers the prognosis for globe salvage. Satellite lesions, ring infiltrates, and endothelial plaques can be seen in moderately severe fungal keratitis.

pool.q: What is distichiasis?

options.a: misdirection of normal eyelashes that curve away from the ocular surface
options.b: misdirection of normal eyelashes that curve toward the ocular surface
options.c: growth of accessory eyelashes posterior to the normal row of eyelashes
options.d: growth of accessory eyelashes anterior to the normal row of eyelashes

pool.rationale: Distichiasis, both congenital and acquired, refers to an accessory row of eyelashes posterior to the normal anatomic location. These can be coarse or fine, and they can occur as a result of numerous inflammatory conditions including Stevens-Johnson syndrome, ocular rosacea, and chemical burns. Misdirected eyelashes arising from the normal anatomic location that curve toward the ocular surface describes trichiasis, not distichiasis. Direction of the eyelashes away from the ocular surface is a normal phenomenon, although it may be exaggerated in the setting of eyelid ectropion.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What class of virus causes molluscum contagiosum?
pool.rationale:
Poxviridae are large, enveloped, double-stranded DNA viruses. Molluscum contagiosum is a poxvirus infection that produces one or more umbilicated nodules on the skin and eyelid margin and, less commonly, on the conjunctiva. These nodules release viral particles that can be found in the tear film and are spread by direct contact with infected individuals.
Ocular manifestations of adenovirus include a follicular conjunctivitis and, less commonly, corneal epithelial keratitis or subepithelial infiltrates. Adenoviruses can cause a broad spectrum of systemic disease, and ocular manifestations most commonly include a follicular conjunctivitis.
Herpesviruses establish latency in their natural host and have a wide variety of ocular manifestations caused by primary infection, recurrent infection, or host inflammatory response. 
The most commonly known parvovirus to infect humans is parvovirus B19, or "fifth disease," which has been associated with some ocular inflammatory manifestations.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient presents with bilateral stromal infiltrates without epithelial ulceration. On review of systems, the patient reports a recent viral upper respiratory tract infection (URI) and difficulty with balance and tinnitus. Rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test and microhemagglutination assay (FTA-ABS) results are negative. What treatment is indicated in addition to the typical therapeutic regimen for this condition?
pool.rationale: This patient's presentation with bilateral nonulcerative stromal inflammation is suggestive of interstitial keratitis, which is an inflammatory, nonulcerative condition primarily involving the corneal stroma. Herpes simplex and syphilis are the most common etiologies of interstitial keratitis in the US. In this case, the negative RPR and FTA-ABS results and a review of systems suggesting vestibuloauditory pathology are consistent with Cogan syndrome, a rare autoimmune disease often precipitated by a viral illness, with features that overlap with polyarteritis nodosa. Cogan syndrome can be associated with vertigo and can lead to permanent deafness if not treated promptly with systemic corticosteroids.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 35-year-old man presents with a 2-day history of decreased vision and of pain in the right eye after being struck by a tree branch while hiking. Vision is 20/50, with an intraocular pressure of 8 mm Hg. Slit-lamp examination is remarkable for a 5-mm vertical conjunctival laceration near the semilunar fold. Examination of the wound is attempted at the slit lamp, but significant bullous subconjunctival hemorrhage limits the examination. What is the best course of management?

options.a: prescription of antibiotics and a follow-up examination in 3 to 5 days
options.b: exploration of the wound with conjunctival peritomy in the operating room
options.c: ultrasonography of the orbits to rule out foreign body
options.d: suture closure of the conjunctival laceration

pool.rationale:
The principal requirement in this setting is to evaluate the wound to its full depth. Since adequate examination in the clinic is halted by subconjunctival hemorrhage, the patient should be taken to the operating room to explore the wound and, if necessary, close an open globe. In addition, the patient's 2-day history of pain and decreased vision should also warrant additional investigation.
Primary closure of the conjunctiva is not advisable without exploration in the setting of trauma with a possible ruptured globe or foreign body: By closing the surface defect, a definitive diagnosis is potentially obscured.
Ultrasonography of an eye should not be performed if there is concern for an open globe, as pressure on the eye could expulse intraocular contents. One could order a computed tomography (CT) scan to examine for any scleral irregularity; however, this is not one of the answer choices.
Treating with antibiotics followed by re-examination in 3 to 5 days is insufficient.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: One day following penetrating keratoplasty with 16 interrupted sutures, a patient is noted to have an aqueous leak originating from the suture track of the 12 o'clock suture. The suture is not visibly loose or malpositioned. The anterior chamber is deep and the pressure is 17 mm Hg. The patient's medications are topical prednisolone acetate 1% QID and topical gentamicin sulfate 0.3% QID.  What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.a: Place a bandage contact lens and start timolol 0.5%.
options.b: Return to the operating room to replace the suture.
options.d: Remove the suture at the slit lamp.

pool.rationale: Suture track leaks generally resolve without surgical intervention and may be monitored closely for spontaneous resolution. Placement of a bandage contact lens and the use of an aqueous suppressant may encourage more rapid closure of the leak. Persistent small wound leaks (those failing to improve after several days of conservative management) or larger wound leaks (those causing significant shallowing of the anterior chamber or iris prolapse) should be repaired in the operating room. Discontinuing topical steroids for a small wound leak is not advisable, and graft rejection may ensue. Unless a suture is broken or overtly loose, it is generally inadvisable to remove the suture in the early postoperative period following penetrating keratoplasty, as doing so may trigger a larger wound dehiscence.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: When considering phototherapeutic keratectomy (PTK) for a corneal scar, what test provides the most objective measurement of the depth of the lesion?
pool.rationale: Anterior segment optical coherence tomography (AS-OCT) provides extremely high-resolution cross-sectional imaging of the corneal layers, which may be beneficial in assessing the depth of a scar prior to attempting phototherapeutic keratectomy. Confocal microscopy can provide in vivo images of different depths of the cornea, but it is not helpful in determining the depth of a scar. Slit-lamp examination is always indicated for the evaluation of a corneal scar but cannot provide the same degree of accuracy with regard to measuring depth as AS-OCT. Ultrasonic pachymetry is useful for measuring total corneal thickness, but it does not allow direct measurement of the depth of a scar.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In a patient with posterior scleritis, what is the most likely finding on B-scan echography?
pool.rationale: Choroidal and scleral thickening are the initial and most consistent findings of posterior scleritis on B-scan ultrasonography. With enough inflammation, patients can also manifest the classic "T-sign," which reflects fluid in sub-Tenon space. Patients with posterior scleritis can also manifest subretinal fluid accumulation with exudative retinal detachments, but this is not as common as choroidal and scleral thickening. Similarly, patients can have optic nerve head edema, but this is not as common on choroidal and scleral thickening. Vitreous opacities are not a finding typically associated with posterior scleritis.

pool.q: What change in the filament of a handheld (Cochet-Bonnet) esthesiometer is required to elicit sensation from a patient with worsening neurotrophic keratopathy?
pool.rationale: Corneal esthesiometry is used to evaluate corneal sensation. The handheld (Cochet-Bonnet) esthesiometer contains a thin, retractable, nylon monofilament that contacts the patient's cornea. Adjusting the length of the monofilament changes the pressure applied by the device. When the filament is shortened, more pressure is applied to the cornea, and less corneal sensation is required to detect the stimulus. When the filament is lengthened, less pressure is applied and more corneal sensation is required to detect stimulus. The thickness of the filament does not change during testing.

pool.q: Incubation of both blood agar and Sabouraud agar media at 25 degrees Celsius can facilitate recovery of what organism?
pool.rationale:
Several recovery techniques are available in cases of suspected fungal infection, including:
  • Staining the specimen with potassium hydroxide, Gram, Giemsa, Gomori-methenamine silver, acridine orange, and/or calcofluor white
  • Plating the specimen on Sabouraud agar in addition to blood agar, chocolate agar, and thioglycollate broth; incubation of media at room temperature (25 degrees Celsius or 77 degrees Fahrenheit) may facilitate fungal recovery as noted specifically by Table 9-4 of the BCSC series. Brain-heart infusion agar can also be used.
  • Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)
Sabouraud agar is specifically meant for fungal organism detection, so it would not detect the other organisms listed. Acanthamoeba would require nonnutrient agar with bacterial overlay, blood agar, or buffered charcoal-yeast extract agar. Neisseria is a gram-negative diplococcus normally seen inside neutrophils on a smear with gram stain, grows on chocolate agar, or can be detected by PCR amplification of its DNA. Chlamydia is an obligate intracellular parasite and is best detected with Giemsa stain, immunofluorescent antibody tests, or by PCR.


(A figure accompanies this rationale on the section page.)

pool.q: A patient has 24 hours of severe, copious conjunctival discharge without a corneal ulcer. Conjunctival gram stain shows numerous neutrophils with gram-negative intracellular diplococci. What is the most appropriate treatment?
pool.rationale: Hyperacute conjunctivitis with gram-negative intracellular (or extracellular) diplococci is diagnostic of gonococcal conjunctivitis caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. If corneal ulceration is present, the patient should be admitted to the hospital to receive intravenous ceftriaxone. In the absence of corneal involvement, outpatient therapy with intramuscular ceftriaxone 1 g and close observation is appropriate. Intravenous penicillin G is indicated for treatment of neurosyphilis. Oral azithromycin is indicated for the treatment of chlamydial conjunctivitis. Topical gentamicin ointment can be used as an adjunctive treatment for gonococcal conjunctivitis, but the mainstay of treatment is systemic ceftriaxone.

pool.q: For acute Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) with conjunctival involvement, what intervention is indicated to reduce long-term formation of symblepharon?

options.b: repeated forniceal debridement with a glass rod

pool.rationale: Early amniotic membrane transplantation has been shown to reduce the formation of symblepharon and minimize the long-term ocular surface complications for patients with conjunctival inflammation from SJS. Symblepharon rings and forniceal debridement have been largely supplanted by amniotic membrane grafting (repeated forniceal debridement may actually worsen conjunctival scarring, owing to mechanical trauma). Temporary tarsorrhaphy may be indicated for non-healing epithelial defects, but it is not directly beneficial to preventing the formation of symblepharon.

pool.q: A patient presents with a Mooren ulcer and sectoral limbal injection. Despite treatment with systemic steroids, progressive corneal thinning is developing adjacent to the area of conjunctival injection, with approximately 25% stromal thickness remaining at the bed of the ulcer. What is the most appropriate therapeutic intervention?
pool.rationale:
Conjunctival resection is indicated for progressive rheumatologic corneal melting disorders that are not responsive to immunosuppression. The presumptive mechanism is distancing the conjunctival vasculature from the area of corneal inflammation. In this case, the focal area of sectoral injection with adjacent corneal thinning allows for relatively easy identification and resection of the responsible tissue.
Limbal stem cell transplantation plays no role in the management of acute corneal melting. Systemic antifungal treatment is not indicated in the absence of a confirmed (or strongly suspected) fungal sclerokeratitis. Penetrating keratoplasty may be indicated in progressive corneal melts, but typically should be delayed unless there is impending (eg, descemetocele) or existing perforation.

pool.q: What kind of pigmented conjunctival lesion could be followed with observation and sequential photographs?

options.a: a nodular, circumscribed, brown lesion of the conjunctiva with prominent vascularity
options.b: flat, poorly circumscribed, brown pigmentation of the bulbar conjunctiva
options.c: large, dark brown pigmentation of the conjunctiva that is increasing in size
options.d: a new, brown, pigmented lesion of the palpebral conjunctiva with signs of inflammation

pool.rationale: Primary acquired melanosis is characterized by flat, brown patches of noncystic pigmentation within the superficial conjunctiva. These lesions may be observed with sequential photographs. Nodularity, enlargement, increased vascularity, or palpebral conjunctival involvement can indicate malignant transformation and should prompt biopsy.

pool.q: What method is usually used to create adherence between a conjunctival flap and the cornea?
pool.rationale:
In the conjunctival flap procedure, conjunctiva is mobilized over the cornea to stabilize inflammatory or structural corneal pathology. Complete debridement of the corneal epithelium helps to create adherence between the conjunctiva and underlying cornea.
Nylon sutures can be used during the procedure to secure the conjunctival flap edges to the sclera. Thermal cautery is an alternative treatment for chronic bullous keratopathy. Cryotherapy can be used on the ocular surface in the setting of malignant lesions, with the goal of reducing recurrence risk while sparing normal tissue.

pool.q: What is the most common bacterial cause of chronic angular blepharoconjunctivitis?
pool.rationale:

pool.q: What infectious agent has an association with conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasia?

pool.q: What illumination technique is based on the property of total internal reflection?
pool.rationale:
Sclerotic scatter is used to detect subtle corneal abnormalities that distort the total internal reflection property of the normal cornea. Decentering the isocentric light beam so that an intense beam shines on the limbus and scatters off the sclera causes a very faint glow of the cornea. Reflective opacities stand out against the dark field, whereas areas of reduced light transmission in the cornea are seen as shades of gray. This technique is effective in demonstrating epithelial edema, mild stromal infiltration, nebulae, and cornea verticillata.
Specular reflection is mainly used to examine corneal endothelium, although it can also be used to examine corneal epithelium and lens epithelium. Direct focal illumination and slit illumination allow detection and localization of structures, including differences in refractive index. Indirect, proximal illumination and lateral illumination purposely focus or reflect the illuminator's light beam at a different, though adjacent, site than the corneal microscope. This technique is useful to highlight abnormalities that have a refractive index similar to their surroundings and that are difficult to discern by direct illumination.

pool.q: A 70-year-old patient presents with right lower eyelid entropion and trouble swallowing. A bilateral blunting of the fornices and a symblepharon are noted on the right side. What is the most appropriate test for this ocular disorder?

Although it is a vesiculobullous disease primarily involving the conjunctiva, it frequently affects other mucous membranes, including those of the mouth and oropharynx, genitalia, and anus. Difficulty swallowing may be an important early symptom. Patients with MMP are usually older than 60 years at the time of diagnosis. They often present with recurrent attacks of mild and nonspecific conjunctival inflammation with an occasional mucopurulent discharge. Patients with early MMP may present with conjunctival hyperemia, edema, ulceration, and tear dysfunction. Transient bullae of the conjunctiva rupture, leading to subepithelial fibrosis. Loss of goblet cells, shortening of the inferior fornices, symblepharon formation, and, on occasion, restricted ocular motility with extensive adhesions between the eyelid and the globe, can follow. Entropion and trichiasis may develop as scarring progresses, leading to abrasions, corneal vascularization, further scarring, ulceration, and epidermalization of the ocular surface. Although MMP is a bilateral disease, one eye may be more severely involved than the other. Pathologic support for a diagnosis of pemphigoid is obtained from direct immunofluorescence or immunoperoxidase staining of conjunctival biopsy specimens.

pool.q: A follicular conjunctivitis with presence of follicles on the bulbar conjunctiva (rather than only the palpebral conjunctiva) is most suggestive of what condition?

The most common medications to cause a toxic conjunctivitis are atropine, antiviral agents, miotics, sulfonamides, alpha-adrenergic agonists, and vasoconstrictors.

pool.q: What clinical appearance of a corneal ulcer is most suggestive of fungal etiology?

In the setting of a corneal ulcer, the presence of multiple infiltrates or smaller "satellite" infiltrates is very suspicious for fungal etiology, especially filamentous fungi (eg, Fusarium, Aspergillus, etc.).
Perineural inflammation may be seen in infections caused by Acanthamoeba.
"Soupy" or wet stromal necrosis and thinning is usually caused by bacterial pathogens, particularly Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

pool.q: A 20-year-old patient presents with a best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) in eyeglasses of 20/100 OU and fine vertical lines in the posterior central cornea on slit-lamp examination. What is the most useful test to confirm the diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
The clinical description is most consistent with keratoconus (the fine vertical lines describe Vogt striae), which is best diagnosed with corneal topography. The expected pattern would be that of asymmetric inferior steepening with high regular and irregular astigmatism.
Specular microscopy allows imaging and quantification of the corneal endothelium, which would be expected to be normal in the setting of keratoconus.
Glare testing may show a decrease in BCVA but is not useful in diagnosing the underlying etiology. It is very helpful for quantifying glare from cataracts, posterior capsule opacity (PCO), and other opacities.
Wavefront analysis would likely show a large degree of lower- and higher-order aberrations. It is mostly used for refractive surgery planning, but it is less often used in the diagnosis of keratoconus, compared to topography.

pool.q: What is the primary treatment for filamentary keratopathy to reduce the severity of recurrence?
pool.rationale:

Filaments should be debrided with a jeweler’s forceps or a cotton swab soaked with topical anesthetic. Treatment directed at enhancing the tear film reduces the severity of recurrence. In addition to tear supplementation and punctal occlusion, acetylcysteine 10%, dispensed with an eyedrop container, can serve as a mucolytic agent and may further reduce filament formation. Topical low-dose corticosteroids, cyclosporine, and therapeutic soft contact lenses may be helpful.
While therapeutic soft contact lenses may be beneficial for treatment of filamentary keratitis due to other causes, bandage soft contact lenses are rarely used to reduce symptoms in patients with ATD, because they may be associated with an increased risk of infection. Patients who use them should therefore be observed carefully. Scleral contact lenses have been found to be extremely helpful in patients with advanced dry eye symptoms.
Hypertonic saline (5% sodium chloride) solution is used for the treatment of recurrent corneal erosions. The drops provide lubrication and may transiently produce an osmotic gradient, drawing fluid from the epithelium and theoretically promoting the adherence of epithelial cells to the underlying tissue.

pool.q: What ocular procedure is contraindicated in a patient with forme fruste keratoconus?

There have been reported cases of ectasia development after PRK, but it is not clear whether this is progression of the underlying disease, or actual hastening because of tissue removal. If the patient shows signs of progression, corneal crosslinking may be an option for stabilization of their corneal condition.

pool.q: What is the classic slit-lamp feature of a neurotrophic corneal ulcer?

The ulcers are typically central or inferior in location (corresponding to areas of maximal exposure) and not typically superior. A single confluent epithelial defect is more commonly seen than multiple discrete epithelial defects.

pool.q: Twelve hours after an endothelial keratoplasty procedure, a patient complains of severe pain, nausea, and vomiting. What is the most likely cause of this problem?
pool.rationale:
All of the choices are potential postoperative complications following endothelial keratoplasty. In the given scenario—early postoperative period with symptoms indicative of elevated intraocular pressure (IOP)—the most likely etiology is pupillary block. Pupillary block following endothelial keratoplasty occurs when the air bubble occludes the pupil and induces secondary angle closure. The typical presentation is that of a flat or very shallow anterior chamber with total or near-total peripheral anterior synechiae. The IOP is typically markedly elevated, and the air bubble may be difficult to discern behind the iris.
Graft dislocation is typically painless and presents with decreased vision and a visibly detached or decentered donor corneal graft, which is usually in the inferior angle.
Endophthalmitis may present with pain, inflammation, and decreased vision, but it would not typically present in the first 24 hours after the surgery with symptoms suggestive of high IOP.
Graft rejection may present, often insidiously, with pain, photophobia, and decreased vision, but it typically does not develop until months or years after the surgery. Again, symptoms of elevated IOP would not typically be present.

pool.q: For the treatment of bullous keratopathy, penetrating keratoplasty may be preferred over endothelial keratoplasty in what situation?

options.a: presence of significant central stromal scarring
options.b: presence of a posterior chamber intraocular lens (IOL)
options.c: previous diagnosis of Fuchs endothelial dystrophy
options.d: previous history of suprachoroidal hemorrhage in fellow eye

pool.rationale:
For most cases of endothelial failure, endothelial keratoplasty--Descemet stripping endothelial keratoplasty (DSEK), Descemet stripping automated endothelial keratoplasty (DSAEK), or Descemet membrane endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK)--is preferred over penetrating keratoplasty. Compared to penetrating keratoplasty, endothelial keratoplasty provides faster visual rehabilitation, lower risk for intraoperative suprachoroidal hemorrhage (due to smaller incision size), and more predictable refractive outcomes.
However, endothelial keratoplasty does not remove central stromal scarring, and penetrating keratoplasty may be necessary to provide optimal visual quality in this situation.
The presence of a posterior chamber intraocular lens or a known history of Fuchs endothelial dystrophy would not affect the decision to perform penetrating keratoplasty in this situation.
A previous suprachoroidal hemorrhage in the fellow eye would favor endothelial keratoplasty for the reasons listed above.

pool.q: What optical phenomenon is used with Placido disk-based topography?
pool.rationale: Placido disk-based topography uses the reflection of a target-shaped image projected onto the patient's cornea. The reflected image has aberrations corresponding to the altered curvature, from which the software calculates keratometric measurements. Chromatic dispersion occurs when white light is unequally refracted into its polychromatic components. This can be bothersome to some patients with high corrections in spectacles. Interferometry can be employed in visual potential assessment by measuring the patient's ability to discriminate between closely spaced lines. Refraction refers to the angle of light as it passes between different media.

pool.q: Conjunctival squamous neoplasia is associated with what medical condition?
pool.rationale:
Systemic immunosuppression is a known risk factor for the development of conjunctival squamous neoplasia. Conjunctival squamous neoplasia in a young adult should prompt further investigation for immune compromise, such as human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. In addition, the neoplasia may be more aggressive in patients with compromised immunity or xeroderma pigmentosum.
Gastrointestinal polyps found in familial adenomatous polyposis or Gardner syndrome are associated with pigmented lesions of the retinal pigment epithelium. Basal nevus syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by multiple nevoid basal cell carcinomas early in life and associated with skeletal anomalies. Patients with Goldenhar syndrome have facial microsomia and can have dermoids, eyelid colobomas (more commonly of the upper eyelid, whereas Treacher-Collins syndrome is associated more with lower eyelid colobomas), microphthalmia, cataract, and iris abnormalities.

pool.q: A 66-year-old man presents for cataract evaluation. On examination, the corneas are clear but have a diameter of ~15 mm. There are visually significant cataracts, but the examination is otherwise normal. The patient is at increased risk for what factor that could complicate cataract surgery?
pool.rationale: Megalocornea is a nonprogressive disorder in which the corneal diameter largely exceeds normal values of less than or equal to 13 mm. Megalocornea is not associated with congenital glaucoma, corneal edema, or opacification. Patients with megalocornea usually develop and retain good vision but can have poor zonular integrity, predisposing them to complications in cataract surgery. Patients with megalocornea do not have increased risk for floppy iris syndrome, choroidal hemorrhage, or prolonged corneal edema with cataract surgery.

pool.q: What is the most common cause of decreased vision in a patient with epithelial basement membrane dystrophy?
pool.rationale:
Visual disturbances in epithelial basement membrane dystrophy (EBMD) are usually caused by irregular astigmatism. For symptomatic patients with irregular astigmatism, epithelial debridement may be necessary; it may also be useful in cases with recurrent corneal erosions.
Corneal haze, edema, and high astigmatism are not often found in this condition. Because different questions will sometimes list a different term for the dystrophy, it is useful to know that the alternate names for EBMD include map-dot-fingerprint dystrophy, Cogan microcystic epithelial dystrophy, and anterior basement membrane dystrophy.

pool.q: What is a common side effect of doxycycline?
pool.rationale:
Oral doxycycline in doses of 40 mg to 200 mg per day is generally well tolerated for external disease, mostly meibomian gland dysfunction. Adverse effects of oral tetracyclines include photosensitization, gastrointestinal upset, and, in rare instances, azotemia. Long-term use may lead to oral or vaginal candidiasis in susceptible patients. The use of tetracyclines is contraindicated during pregnancy, in women who are breastfeeding, and in patients with a known hypersensitivity to these agents. These antibiotics should be avoided in children younger than 8 years because they cause permanent discoloration of teeth and bones in this population.
Photophobia, blurred vision and onychomycosis would be very uncommon from doxycycline.
"Increased risk of sunburn" or "vaginal yeast infection" are other possible correct answers. Azotemia and intracranial hypertension are also possible but not common.

pool.q: An adult patient who suffered a severe unilateral alkali injury to his right eye developed progressive pannus, conjunctival epithelialization of the cornea, and a central persistent epithelial defect, despite appropriate treatment. What is the most appropriate surgical option for visual improvement?
pool.rationale:
The clinical scenario describes a unilateral limbal stem cell deficiency after an alkali injury. Since the limbal stem cells of the other eye were not affected, a conjunctival limbal autograft can be performed. In this procedure, healthy limbal stem cells are harvested from the unaffected eye and transplanted to the affected eye of the same patient.
If there is loss of limbal stem cells bilaterally, a patient may receive stem cells from an eye bank donor cornea via a keratolimbal allograft (KLAL). A KLAL has a higher risk of rejection than a conjunctival limbal autograft and requires systemic immunosuppression. A penetrating keratoplasty requires healthy stem cells to maintain a clear graft. A superficial keratectomy could be performed to clear the pannus and conjunctival epithelium but requires healthy limbal stem cells to maintain a clear cornea. Likewise, a penetrating keratoplasty requires healthy limbal stem cells to maintain a clear graft.

pool.q: A patient who has had a corneal transplant complains of decreased vision. Corneal topography can identify what issue in a previously transplanted cornea?
pool.rationale: Corneal topography is a structural, not a functional test. It will identify irregular astigmatism, including ectasias. Specular microscopy can be used to quantify loss of endothelial cells. Tomography is required to examine the posterior corneal curvature. Corneal topography may detect regions of corneal edema change, but it is not capable of detecting corneal transplant rejection or endothelial cell viability.

pool.q: The outcomes of what surgery could theoretically be improved by sophisticated measurements of corneal hysteresis?

options.d: phacoemulsification with implantation of multifocal intraocular lenses

pool.rationale: Corneal hysteresis is the difference between the pressure at which the cornea bends inward with air-jet applanation and the pressure at which it bends outward again. It gauges elasticity of the cornea. Theoretically, accurate measurement of this biomechanical property would identify corneas at risk for ectasia during laser refractive surgery such as LASIK or photorefractive keratectomy (PRK).

pool.q: What is the most common complication of a conjunctival flap?
pool.rationale:
The most common complication of conjunctival flaps is retraction of the flap, which occurs in approximately 10% of cases. To lower the risk of retraction, the surgeon should take care to minimize tension on any conjunctival flap when it is placed.
Hemorrhage beneath the flap and formation of epithelial inclusion cysts are other possible complications of a conjunctival flap but are less common than retraction. Ptosis may occur after a conjunctival flap but may or may not be related to the flap itself.

pool.q: A young adult presents with a chronic red right eye. His previous treatments for dry eye have not worked. He has a small fleshy pink lesion near the limbus. He has had night sweats and lost weight over the past year. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
This patient has systemic symptoms of weight loss and a pink mass that are typical for conjunctival lymphoma. Usually described as a "salmon patch," a conjunctival lymphoma lesion can be seen near the limbus or in the fornix region. Chronic redness is possible. HIV disease can be a risk factor. The other answer choices (squamous cell carcinoma of conjunctiva, sarcoidosis, and amyloidosis) are in the differential but are not correct. The night sweats and weight loss are helpful in identifying this patient as a potential lymphoma patient.
Other ocular surface squamous lesions are in the differential as well. Treatment depends on whether systemic disease is present. Night sweats are a common symptom of lymphoma, but not of the other conditions. Squamous cell carcinoma presents with a white or yellowish pink lesion near the limbus with possibly leukoplakia. This rarely metastasizes. Amyloidosis of conjunctiva usually presents with a waxy yellowish localized lesion.

pool.q: Peripheral ulcerative keratitis can be associated with what gastrointestinal disease?
pool.rationale:
Peripheral ulcerative keratitis (PUK) is associated with many autoimmune conditions, and can cause keratolysis, or melting of the corneal stroma, typically peripherally. It can be found in such diseases as rheumatoid arthritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly called Wegener granulomatosis), relapsing polychondritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and inflammatory bowel disease (both Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis). Irritable bowel syndrome, peptic ulcer disease, and celiac sprue are not associated with PUK.

pool.q: What is the typical conjunctival finding in atopic keratoconjunctivitis (AKC)?
pool.rationale:
AKC is characterized by the presence of chronic inflammation, small or medium-sized papillae, and milky conjunctival edema with possible subepithelial fibrosis. Corneal neovascularization, punctate staining, and/or corneal epithelial defects are commonly seen.
Giant papillary reactions are associated with vernal keratoconjunctivitis rather than atopic disease. Follicles can occur with several infections, including viral and chlamydial infections, and can also occur with medications. However, they are not associated with atopic disease.

pool.q: A newborn baby is noted to have bilateral, central corneal opacities. Ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM) shows iris and lenticular adhesions to the cornea. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
The stem describes Peters anomaly, which is characterized by the presence of a central or paracentral corneal opacity at birth. This is due to the localized absence of the corneal endothelium. Peters anomaly type I is characterized by iridocorneal adhesions, and Peters anomaly type II is characterized by corneolenticular adhesions. Glaucoma is present in 50% of patients with the condition.
Congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy (CHED) is characterized by thickening of Descemet membrane, with sparse, atrophic corneal endothelial cells. Posterior embryotoxon involves a thickened and anteriorly displaced Schwalbe line. Sclerocornea is a nonprogressive, noninflammatory scleralization of the cornea. Sclerocornea, CHED, and posterior embryotoxon can all manifest as a cloudy cornea but do not have iris or lenticular adhesion to the cornea.

pool.q: Lattice corneal dystrophy is characterized by the deposition of what material in the corneal stroma?
pool.rationale:
Lattice corneal dystrophy is a bilateral autosomal dominant condition, with the deposition of amyloid within the central corneal stroma. It is a form of primary localized amyloidosis. The amyloid forms typical branching linear opacities and is deposited by the epithelial and stromal cells, most heavily in the anterior stroma. Pathologically, the amyloid is visible in hematoxylin and eosin stains as eosinophilic fusiform deposits, which stain positive with Congo red and show metachromasia with crystal violet. Amyloid exhibits dichroism and "apple-green" birefringence with polarized light. Lattice dystrophy may recur in corneal grafts. The TGFB1 (formerly BIGH3) gene has been shown to undergo multiple mutations, which can variably lead to Reis-Bückler, Avellino, granular, or lattice dystrophy.
There are 4 subtypes of lattice corneal dystrophy. Type I is the classic variant, with visual or corneal epithelial abrasions by the end of the first decade. It is linked to 5q31, with type A amyloid. Type II (Meretoja syndrome) shows symptoms by the end of the second decade and is associated with mask-like facial features, blepharochalasis, cranial and peripheral nerve palsies, and dry, lax skin. A mutation at 9q34 in the gelsolin gene has been identified. The familial form has been described in Scandinavian families. In Type III, deposits are type AP amyloid, with a later onset, possibly autosomal recessive inheritance, and deeper, larger deposits of amyloid. In Type IV, deposits are larger, deeper, and more nodular, occurring only in later life with mild visual disturbance.

pool.q: What antifungal agent is indicated as first-line treatment of superficial keratitis caused by Fusarium species?
pool.rationale: Natamycin is generally considered first-line therapy for most cases of fungal keratitis due to infection with filamentous fungi (eg, Fusarium species). Amphotericin B is preferred for treatment of yeast keratitis (eg, Candida). Voriconazole is efficacious against a variety of fungal infections, but it was shown to be inferior to natamycin in a prospective, randomized clinical trial. Fluconazole has largely been replaced by newer azoles (voriconazole, posaconazole) because of their improved ocular penetration with systemic administration. Of note, ocular penetration through intact corneal epithelium is poor for many antifungal agents, including natamycin; for deep lesions, serial epithelial debridement might be indicated to enhance tissue penetration.

pool.q: By what route is cytomegalovirus (CMV) typically transmitted?
pool.rationale:
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a DNA virus from the herpes family that causes subclinical infections in children and a nonspecific febrile illness in adults. The virus becomes latent in the CD34+ myeloid progenitor cells, which can then be activated and allow for shedding of the virus. CMV manifests in the eye most commonly as a sectoral, necrotizing retinitis in immunocompromised patients. It can present in the anterior chamber and cornea as fine stellate keratic precipitates, epithelial and stromal keratitis, and endotheliitis. The risk of contracting CMV through casual contact is very small. The virus is passed through body fluids such as saliva or breast milk or through sexual contact.
Adenoviruses, which can cause follicular conjunctivitis, pharyngoconjunctival fever, and epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC), are transmitted by close contact with ocular or respiratory secretions or contaminated fomites. Varicella-zoster virus (VZV), which can present as a dermatomal vesicular dermatitis, follicular conjunctivitis, keratitis, or acute retinal necrosis, can be spread by direct contact with VZV skin lesions or respiratory secretions via airborne droplets. The fecal-oral route of disease transmission is seen in toxoplasmosis and toxocariasis.

pool.q: A 45-year-old man presents with decreased vision in the right eye from an old ocular injury. On examination, there is scarring in the mid-posterior stroma of his cornea, located in the visual axis, severely limiting vision. The patient is interested in improving his eyesight. What anterior segment procedure can best treat his pathology?
pool.rationale:
Deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty is a surgical procedure in which corneal tissue is excised down to the Descemet membrane, with replacement through transplanted corneal donor tissue. This procedure can be used in treatment of keratoconus, corneal dystrophies, and deep stromal corneal scars. It confers some advantage over penetrating keratoplasty by leaving the Descemet membrane and endothelium intact, preventing the risk of endothelial rejection. Additionally, because full-thickness corneal incisions are not needed, there is less risk of expulsive hemorrhage, retinal detachment, or cystoid macular edema.
Phototherapeutic keratectomy and superficial keratectomy can be utilized for more superficial pathology in the subepithelial layer, Bowman layer, or anterior stroma. Endothelial keratoplasty would confer little benefit in this patient.

pool.q: An 11-year-old girl presents with a unilateral granulomatous conjunctivitis accompanied by a tender submandibular lymphadenopathy and low-grade fever. What is the most likely etiology?
pool.rationale:
Bartonella henselae

The presentation is that of Parinaud oculoglandular syndrome: unilateral granulomatous conjunctivitis with regional lymphadenopathy. The lymphadenopathy may occur concurrently with conjunctivitis or 1 to 2 weeks following. The primary causative agent is Bartonella henselae, which may be transmitted by a cat-scratch injury, and serology can be used in confirming the diagnosis. While no definitive standard is established for antibiotic treatment, azithromycin, doxycycline, and erythromycin are common choices.
Chlamydia trachomatis, Borrelia burgdorferi, and adenovirus are causes of follicular conjunctivitis.

pool.q: For what corneal disorder is deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty an appropriate procedure?

options.c: keratoconus with a history of hydrops

pool.rationale: Deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty (DALK) is appropriate in cases where the corneal abnormality is limited to the stroma, with normal Descemet membrane and endothelium. As such, granular dystrophy is the most appropriate choice. Lesions in granular corneal dystrophy involve the superficial stroma and mid-stroma.

pool.q: A 12-year-old boy from the Dominican Republic is referred to an ophthalmologist for evaluation. His primary care doctor noted significant darkening of his bilateral medial and lateral recti muscle insertions as well as the adjacent sclera. Furthermore, there is a similar darkening of his earlobes and nose. What urine abnormality is this patient most likely to have?

options.d: urine that turns dark when exposed to air

pool.rationale: This patient has examination findings consistent with ochronosis. Ochronosis is seen in alkaptonuria, a disease of tyrosine and phenylalanine metabolism deficiency, which leads to the accumulation of alkapton, a brownish/blackish material, in body tissues. Homogentisic acid accumulates in the body. Common tissues affected include the medial and lateral recti and cartilaginous tissues such as earlobes, the nose, heart valves, and tendons. This condition is seen most frequently in patients from the Dominican Republic and from Slovakia. The urine in these patients will turn dark after exposure to air. These patients frequently complain of arthropathy, which high-dose ascorbic acid can help alleviate.

pool.q: A 19-year-old man is referred for evaluation of ectopia lentis. The patient has a tall, thin appearance with kyphoscoliosis and abnormally long and slender fingers. The patient reports that he has not been to a doctor since he was a young child and has no known systemic abnormalities. Aside from treatment of the ectopia lentis, the patient must be referred for workup of what potentially fatal systemic association?
pool.rationale: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the FBN1 gene, which encodes fibrillin. It is associated with disorders of the eye, skeletal system, and heart. Ectopia lentis is an eye finding that is classically associated with Marfan syndrome. A cardiac evaluation is necessary to look for aortic dilation or aneurysms that can cause premature mortality in Marfan patients.

pool.q: For a patient with Thygeson superficial punctate keratitis, what is the recommended initial management?
pool.rationale: Thygeson superficial punctate keratitis is characterized by multiple, slightly elevated corneal epithelial lesions with negative staining. This can be accompanied by symptoms of foreign-body sensation, photophobia, tearing, and reduced vision. These lesions usually regress rapidly with the use of mild corticosteroids but can recur after tapering. Supportive therapy with artificial tears is often adequate in mild initial cases. Topical steroids can hasten the lesions' resolution, but use of these drugs should be minimized because the lesions often recur after the steroids are tapered. Topical cyclosporine or tacrolimus ophthalmic preparations may also be effective in causing regression of the lesions.

pool.q: What is the most likely diagnosis for a patient with bilateral crusting of the eyelashes, eyelid margin telangiectasias, papillary conjunctivitis, and peripheral corneal infiltrates?
pool.rationale: The description is classic for staphylococcal blepharoconjunctivitis. Herpes simplex blepharoconjunctivitis is characterized by a follicular conjunctival reaction, vesicular eyelid skin, or ulcerated eyelid margin lesions, and often preauricular lymphadenopathy. It is almost always unilateral, except in patients with underlying immunodeficiency or atopic disease. Vernal keratoconjunctivitis can present with bilateral papillary conjunctivitis (it is typically severe enough to be labeled "giant" papillary conjunctivitis). However, crusting of the eyelashes and eyelid margin telangiectasia are not typical features. Floppy eyelid syndrome can also cause a velvety upper lid papillary reaction, but marginal corneal infiltrates are not typical.

pool.q: Superior limbal keratoconjunctivitis (SLK) is characterized by what pattern of fluorescein staining?

options.a: corneal staining at 3 o'clock and 9 o'clock

pool.rationale:
Different disease states can produce various punctate staining patterns. Superior limbal corneal staining may be seen with SLK, upper eyelid foreign body, trichiasis, or localized superior limbal stem cell deficiency.
SLK is a chronic, recurrent condition characterized by ocular irritation and injection superiorly. Ocular findings include fine papillary reaction on the superior tarsal conjunctiva, injection and thickening of the superior bulbar conjunctiva, hypertrophy of the superior limbus, superior filamentary keratitis, or fine punctate fluorescein, lissamine green, or rose bengal staining of the superior bulbar conjunctiva above the limbus with involvement of the superior cornea just below the limbus.
Corneal staining at 3 o'clock and 9 o'clock is typical of contact lens wear. Interpalpebral staining is typical of dry eye disease, exposure, and neurotrophic keratopathy. Diffuse punctate staining is typical of viral conjunctivitis, trauma, or toxicity.

pool.q: A 24-year-old female presents with a foreign body sensation and irritation of her right eye. On examination, the ophthalmologist notes trichiasis of the right lower lid with 2 aberrant eyelashes. The patient wants to have the lashes removed for the greatest duration possible without causing any collateral damage to the lid. What treatment would meet this criterion?
pool.rationale: Electrolysis with a radiofrequency probe is useful for removing a few eyelashes at a time and is most effective at preventing recurrence without causing collateral damage. Eyelashes removed by cutting grow back quickly, and lashes removed by epilation can recur in as few as 3 weeks. Cryotherapy can also be used to treat trichiasis, but can cause eyelid margin thinning, loss of adjacent normal lashes, and depigmentation.

pool.q: During treatment and recovery from a corneal abrasion, a patient develops a chalky white plaque covering the extent of the abrasion and obscuring the visual axis. What is the most likely medication being used?
pool.rationale: Use of topical fluoroquinolones, especially ciprofloxacin, can result in chalky white deposits that adhere to corneal epithelial defects. A major factor in drug deposition is pH-dependent solubility of the drug. Also, patients with dry eye using eyedrops more frequently and for a prolonged period are prone to drug precipitation. Corneal deposits are more common in the interpalpebral region because of ultraviolet radiation–induced corneal damage and because of the maximum accumulation of topical ophthalmic medications in this part of the eye. These cases can be managed conservatively, avoiding debridement; deposits resolve after discontinuation of the medication.

pool.q: What is the most common adverse reaction caused by topical trifluridine drops for the treatment of herpes simplex virus (HSV) keratitis?
pool.rationale:
Epithelial toxicity is a common adverse reaction caused by the frequent administration of topical trifluridine for the treatment of herpes simplex keratitis. It should be suspected in patients with nonhealing epithelial defects or worsening epitheliopathy. When epithelial toxicity is found, the medication should be discontinued or replaced with oral antiviral prophylaxis (eg, acyclovir, valacyclovir).
Increased iris pigmentation can be caused by administration of topical prostaglandin analogues.
Induced myopia can be seen in patients taking oral topiramate.
Follicular conjunctivitis, not papillary conjunctivitis, appears as a toxic reaction in some patients receiving topical trifluridine.

pool.q: A 34-year-old man has a hyphema after being struck in the right eye with a tennis ball. Primary therapy should include what intervention?

options.a: instruct the patient to maintain a supine position

pool.rationale: Topical steroid therapy is frequently employed in the traumatic hyphema patient. Topical corticosteroids are beneficial in controlling anterior chamber inflammation and preventing synechiae formation, and they may play a role in preventing rebleeding. Topical cycloplegics are also recommended, not miotics such as pilocarpine. Patients should adopt an elevated position, not supine. Nonaspirin analgesics should be used for pain relief to reduce the risk of rebleeding.

pool.q: What process precedes Salzmann nodular degeneration?
pool.rationale: Salzmann nodular degeneration represents postinflammatory deposition of hyaline and fibrillar material, which replaces the Bowman layer. Oftentimes, patients have a history of corneal trauma, trachoma, corneal surgery, recurrent corneal erosions, or contact lens wear, but other patients present with nodules without any of these risk factors. Calcium deposition is seen in band keratopathy. Genetic dystrophies would result from mutations in various genes such as the TGFB1 gene in lattice corneal dystrophy. Lipid deposition can be seen with corneal neovascularization, which can occur following various types of keratitis; however, the Salzmann nodules do not contain lipid.

pool.q: What  preoperative test is most helpful when considering peripheral corneal relaxing incisions for the treatment of astigmatism at the time of cataract surgery?
pool.rationale:
Limbal relaxing incisions (LRI) can correct the astigmatism contributed by the cornea. A preoperative topography reveals how much astigmatism there is and whether it is regular. Irregular astigmatism cannot be corrected as well by LRIs.

Manifest refraction includes both lenticular and corneal astigmatism and would not be useful on LRIs performed during cataract surgery as the natural lens is removed. 
Specular microscopy is used to evaluate the endothelium and contributes less to the evaluation of astigmatism.

Hartmann-Shack aberrometry is a wavefront analyzer that describes the optical aberrations of the eye for use in wavefront-guided laser refractive surgery.
